author: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
hunk_contexts: A growable array of characters for the part of a token that an input adapter
message:
* Keep only the beginning and the end of a long token for error messages

For "last read" in parse errors, the lexer keeps the text of the token it
reads. The token start moves only at strings and numbers, so everything
after a string or number belongs to it until the next one starts. Input
that cannot be read again copies that text while parsing (the istream and
FILE* adapters in their carry buffer, the lexer in token_string for
iterators), so valid input of 1 followed by 100,000,000 newlines peaked
at about 225 MB, and a long string was kept a second time.

Replace the carry buffer and token_string by token_text_buffer, which
keeps the first 4096 and at least the last 4112 characters of a token and
drops the characters in between where it would otherwise grow, so
appending stays as cheap as before. get_token_string() shows a token of
more than 8192 characters as its first and last 4096 characters around
"...", the same for every kind of input; contiguous input copies only
these parts.

The example input now peaks at 1.8 MB. Instruction counts of parsing
from std::string, std::istream and FILE* are unchanged (clang 21 and
GCC 15); parsing from std::list<char> needs 1 to 17 % fewer.

Fixes #6120.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Suppress an Infer false positive in the token text buffer test

author: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
message:
* Use CMake 4.5's stable import std support in the module test

CMake 4.5 makes `import std` available to every target that scans for
C++ modules and drops the experimental CMAKE_EXPERIMENTAL_CXX_IMPORT_STD
gate and the CXX_MODULE_STD property. The module test no longer needs the
version-specific opt-in token, so the ci_module_cpp20 jobs no longer have
to pin CMake 4.3.4 and now request CMake ^4.5.0.

The modules, CMake and README documentation now list the CMake, generator
and toolchain requirements for building the module and for `import std;`.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Bump lukka/get-cmake from 4.4.5 to 4.5.0

get-cmake 4.4.5 does not know CMake 4.5.0, so the ci_module_cpp20 jobs
that request '^4.5.0' failed in the setup step. Bump every pin so all
jobs use the same action version.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Install unzip in the Clang module job before get-cmake

The ^4.5.0 CMake/Ninja cache key is new, so get-cmake has to unzip the
Ninja download, and silkeh/clang:latest has no unzip.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Disable C++ module scanning for the unit tests

With CMake 4.5, every target that scans for C++ modules gets a synthesized
std module target. For the C++20 and newer unit-test targets, this compiled
libstdc++'s std.cc with the -Werror test flags and failed to configure with
libc++ images that lack std.compat.cppm. The unit tests use no modules, so
turn scanning off; the module test is a separate project.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

subject: Use CMake 4.5's stable import std support in the module test (#6103)

author: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
message:
* Make unflatten() linear in the length of the keys

unflatten() decides in a first pass which prefixes of the keys denote arrays
(those that have a reference token 0 among their children), and looks up
prefixes again in the second pass. A prefix was identified by hashing it, and
by comparing it byte by byte with the entry in the set, from its beginning.
A key with n tokens therefore cost n^2/2 bytes: 100,000 tokens "/0" took
2.4 s (3.12.0: 5 ms), and so did "/0" followed by "/1" tokens, because every
new level looks its prefix up. Keys in the order of an unsorted object type
(ordered_json) defeated the shortcut for keys that share a beginning with the
previous one: four keys were enough to be quadratic.

Prefixes of less than 64 bytes are kept in a hash table and compared as
before, which costs a bounded number of bytes. Longer prefixes are kept in a
tree whose nodes are looked up by their parent and the text of one token. The
node of a prefix is found by walking the tokens of the key from the root, so
all prefixes of a key together cost one pass over the key, and no prefix is
compared as a whole. The nodes along the key walked last are kept, so keys
that share a beginning do not walk it again. The array/object decision and
the independence from the order of the keys are unchanged.

The hash function is seeded with a value derived from the address of a local
variable, which address space layout randomization changes between
processes, so keys cannot be crafted to collide in advance: with the fixed
constants, 20,000 keys of 16 + 2 bytes with the same hash took 0.5 s (random
keys, and 3.12.0: 7 ms). Where addresses are not randomized, or when the seed
is known, k short prefixes can still collide and cost k^2 / 2 comparisons of
fewer than 64 bytes. Results do not depend on the seed.

Measurements (Apple clang -O2, arm64), unflatten() of one key with n tokens:

  tokens "/0"          n=25k  n=50k  n=100k  n=200k
  before              175 ms 617 ms 2437 ms 9729 ms
  after                 4 ms   6 ms   12 ms   27 ms
  3.12.0                1 ms   3 ms    5 ms   10 ms

  "/0" then "/1"       n=25k  n=50k  n=100k  n=200k
  before              153 ms 603 ms 2436 ms 9678 ms
  after                 1 ms   3 ms    5 ms   10 ms
  3.12.0                1 ms   3 ms    5 ms   11 ms

  ordered_json, 4 keys /0*m/a0, /10, /0*m/a1, /11
                       m=25k  m=50k  m=100k  m=200k
  before              397 ms 1402 ms 5191 ms 20723 ms
  after                 4 ms   7 ms   15 ms   33 ms
  3.12.0                2 ms   3 ms    8 ms   17 ms

Ordinary documents (flatten() then unflatten(), instructions retired): within
0.3 % of before for canada, citm_catalog, twitter, jeopardy, mesh,
update-center and random from the benchmark corpus.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Fix -Wuseless-cast in array_prefix_set::reseed

uintptr_t is already uint64_t on LP64 Linux, so the explicit cast is
useless there; rely on the implicit (widening) conversion instead.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Throw type_error.313 when an unflatten key is a prefix of an earlier key

With an object type that keeps the insertion order (ordered_json), a key
such as "/a" can come after "/a/b". The final assignment then replaced the
object built for "/a/b" without an error, so {"/a/b":2,"/a":1} gave
{"a":1}. json never saw this because std::map visits the shorter key first.

Throw type_error.313 if the target of the final assignment is no longer
null, as json does for the same members. A null value keeps the container,
so {"/a/b":2,"/a":null} gives {"a":{"b":2}} for both object types.

Fixes #6105.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

author: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
hunk_contexts: own, so on its own it lets 9 bytes announce 1048576 values, and every further
auto reserve_array(ArrayType& arr, std::size_t len, priority_tag<1> /*unused*/)
message:
* Bound the total number of valueless UBJSON elements per input

An optimized UBJSON array of type Z, T or F has no payload, so its
declared count is not bounded by the input. The limit of 1048576 applied
to each array on its own, so 9 bytes (`[$Z#l` and a count) produced
1048576 values and every further 9 bytes another 1048576: 362 bytes
allocated 661 MB in a DOM, and a SAX handler received 1M events per 9
bytes.

The reader now adds the counts of all such arrays of one input and
rejects the input with out_of_range.408 when the sum exceeds 1048576
plus 4 for every byte read so far. The base is the per-array limit, so
an array that was accepted on its own before is still accepted at the
start of an input. These arrays add about 80 bytes of memory per input
byte (measured 77; one `Z` per byte needs 32), plus the base; the memory
of a document as a whole is not bounded by this. The check runs once per
valueless array, before its start event, with plain size_t arithmetic
that cannot overflow for a 32-bit size_t. Containers with a payload type
and objects (every member needs a key) are bounded by the input already
and are unchanged. BJData rejects these types.

to_ubjson counts the elements of the typed arrays it writes in one call
and writes an array in the unoptimized form (`[#n Z Z ...`) once it would
bring the total above 1048576, which a reader accepts at any input size.
The check is made only for a typed array of a valueless type, so BJData
and other arrays do not pay for it. Everything to_ubjson writes in
version 3.13.0 can therefore be read back.

Two consequences:
- to_ubjson output changes for values with more than 1048576 elements in
  arrays of type Z, T or F: such an array is written at one byte per
  element, e.g. 270000 rows of 100 nulls take 26.8 MB instead of 1.35 MB.
- Output of version 3.12.0 and earlier (typed arrays without such a
  total) is rejected by from_ubjson when the arrays hold more than
  1048576 elements plus 4 per byte of input. 3.12.0 writes a row of up to 255 nulls in 5 bytes (6 above
  255), so a table is rejected from 1075 rows of 1000 nulls or 209723
  rows of 25 (accepted: 1000 rows of 1000, 209000 rows of 25); rows of
  20 or fewer are never rejected.

Measured on the test data: no file of json_test_data (converted with
to_ubjson in all three modes, 846 round trips) holds an array of this
kind with more than 0.17 values per byte. All of them are read back.

Reproducer (K arrays of 1048576 nulls), Apple clang -O2:
  K=40 (362 bytes): before 41943040 values, 664 MB; after rejected, 33 MB
  K=2 (20 bytes):   before 2097152 values, 53 MB;   after rejected, 33 MB

The new tests count events with a SAX handler where they can: building
and comparing million-element values made the first version take 176 s
under Valgrind, the current one about 22 s.

Behaviour change: an input that holds more than 1048576 elements in
arrays of type Z, T or F at more than 4 per byte is now rejected.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Report an empty array for UBJSON `[$N#<n>` instead of n elements

A no-op (N) is not a value, so an optimized array of type N holds no
element whatever count it declares. The reader skipped the elements but
still passed the declared count to the SAX parser: a handler was told
start_array(n) and no element followed, and the DOM parser reserved
min(n, 16384) values (256 KB) for an array that stays empty. Nine bytes
(`[$N#l 0x7FFFFFFF`) therefore committed 256 KB: 2000 of them in one
input, 18 KB, committed 512 MB of heap (capacity 163,840,000 values for
the 10000 arrays of the original probe: 2.6 GB for 70 KB of input).
Untouched pages keep the resident size small, but the commit charge and
a 32-bit address space are consumed.

The reader now announces 0 elements for an optimized array of type N.
The loop that skips the elements is unchanged (it never ran). A count
that does not fit into std::size_t is still rejected by the count
reader; a count that is too large for the array type of the DOM (before:
out_of_range.408 "excessive array size" from the DOM handler) is
accepted now, because the array is empty.

Behaviour change: sax_parse reports start_array(0) for `[$N#n` (before:
n); from_ubjson no longer throws out_of_range.408 for an N-typed array
whose count exceeds the maximum size of the array type.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Bound what the DOM parsers reserve for arrays that announce a size

Cause: #5476 made the DOM parsers reserve storage (up to 16384 elements)
for a counted array of CBOR, MessagePack, UBJSON and BJData when it
opens, before any input backs the count. The arrays that are open at the
same time keep their storage until the parse ends, so N nested headers
that announce 16384 elements and are never completed hold
N * 16384 * sizeof(json): 100,000 nested CBOR headers `99 40 00`
(300,000 bytes) peaked at 1.65 GiB, 3.12.0 at 12 MiB; the same for
MessagePack `DC 40 00`, UBJSON `[#I 16384` and BJData.

Fix: json_sax_dom_error_state, the base of the three DOM parsers, keeps a
credit of elements that may still be reserved: 65,536 at the start plus
2 for every byte the reader has read. An array that announces no more
than the credit left is reserved as before (one comparison and one
subtraction per counted array); a larger one is reserved what is left
and grows as its elements arrive. binary_reader tells a DOM parser (a
handler whose pointer converts to json_sax_dom_error_state*; a handler
that derives from one privately or protectedly, or any other SAX handler,
is not told anything and reserves as in the base of this change) where to
find its count of characters read for the duration of sax_parse(). An
RAII guard puts back the previous binding on every exit, also by
exception, so the parser never keeps a pointer to a reader that is gone
(unbound, only the per-array cap of 16384 applies); the public SAX
interface is unchanged, and start_array() still reports the announced number. A
bound per array by the remaining input would not help, since the same
bytes would back every open level; the bound has to be over all arrays.

The elements of an array take at least one byte of input each, so the
credit is more than honest input needs: none of the 19 inputs measured
(canada, citm_catalog, twitter, mesh, update-center, random, numbers,
animation, ik_rig, instruments, geo_response, jeopardy and 7 synthetic
ones, each as CBOR, MessagePack, UBJSON and BJData, with and without
size/type optimization) was given less than it announced. A value that
nests five or more arrays of 16384 elements, each with an array as its
first element, is the exception: the later ones grow as before.

Measurements (clang -O2, macOS arm64, peak memory footprint of
`/usr/bin/time -l`, reproducer: n nested headers):

              n = 20,000                n = 100,000
              develop   fix   3.12.0   develop    fix   3.12.0
  CBOR        338.7    5.9    8.2      1687.7    23.3   11.8   MiB
  MessagePack 338.9    6.0    7.3      1687.9    23.8   11.9   MiB
  UBJSON      339.0    7.6    8.0      1687.9    30.1   11.6   MiB
  BJData      339.0    7.3    7.9      1688.0    30.8   11.6   MiB

That is at most (65,536 + 2 per input byte) values: 1 MiB plus 32 bytes
per input byte with 16-byte values (a value is 24 bytes with
JSON_DIAGNOSTICS and up to 40 with JSON_DIAGNOSTIC_POSITIONS), as
documented in untrusted_input.md. Lower fixed caps do not get there: a
cap of 64 elements still peaks at 113 MiB (n = 100,000) and costs 4.7 %
on arrays of 300 elements (mat300.cbor) and 5.0 % on arrays of 10,000
(arrays_of_big.cbor).

Reader instructions retired (min of 7, 108 rows: 18 inputs in the 6 forms
CBOR, MessagePack, UBJSON and BJData plain and optimized; jeopardy, 46 MB,
is within 0.1 %), compared with the base of this change: -0.19 % to +0.37 % in the formats that announce
sizes (canada.cbor 81.9 M -> 82.1 M, many_small.cbor 333.5 M -> 334.2 M);
the benefit of #5476 is kept (without any reserve canada.cbor takes
116.8 M, +42.6 %, many_small.cbor +71.5 %, mat300.cbor +81.6 %). Rows of
plain UBJSON and BJData, whose arrays announce no size, move by -2.7 % to
+2.6 % without any code of theirs changing: the base alternates
between two instruction counts per process (452 M and 463 M for
many_pairs.ubjson, equal in cycles), and a struct with three unused
members added to the same class reproduces the 474 M mode.

Tests (CBOR, MessagePack, UBJSON, BJData): 200 nested headers that
announce 16384 elements peak at 52,433,600 bytes of DOM allocations on
the base and below 128 Ki values with the fix (scaled by sizeof(value),
so that it holds with the diagnostic macros) (counting allocator, no
process memory measured); an array that completes is still reserved in
one allocation; CBOR also checks that a DOM parser is not bound to a finished
parse (ASan: stack-use-after-scope without the guard), that wrappers
derived publicly (also with a parse inside the parse), privately and
protectedly compile and are bound or not as described, that an array that got less than it
announced decodes and that a SAX handler is told the announced size.
The new tests take 4.6 s under Valgrind at -O0 (gcc:12, all four files).

* Add JSON_UBJSON_VALUELESS_ELEMENTS_PER_BYTE to set the UBJSON whole-input budget (#6083)

* Add JSON_UBJSON_VALUELESS_ELEMENTS_PER_BYTE to set the UBJSON whole-input budget

The whole-input budget for the elements of optimized UBJSON arrays of
type Z, T and F (1048576 plus 4 per byte read) rejects files written by
3.12.0 that have long arrays of these types, such as 1100 rows of 1000
nulls with a `$Z` annotation, and there was no way to read them. The
per-byte rate is now the macro JSON_UBJSON_VALUELESS_ELEMENTS_PER_BYTE.

Semantics:
- default 4, so the default build is unchanged (the generated code of
  from_ubjson is identical at -O2 up to source line numbers);
- the value must be a positive integer: 0, negative, non-integral, bool,
  character and wider-than-uintmax_t values fail to compile with a
  static_assert that names the macro;
- a value that does not fit into std::size_t is the largest size_t, so
  one spelling works for 32- and 64-bit targets;
- the limit base + rate * bytes_read saturates at the largest size_t
  instead of wrapping around, for any rate and input size; a rate of
  131072 (2^20 / 8) or more cannot be exceeded by any input (the
  shortest header of an array of more than 32767 elements is 8 bytes),
  which switches the whole-input budget off;
- the limit of one array (1048576) and the base (1048576) stay fixed
  constants, so the writer fallback still follows the base only and a
  reader with any rate reads everything the writer produces;
- the macro is not part of the ABI tag and must have the same value in
  every translation unit; it is documented that way.

The memory the arrays can take in a DOM is about 20 bytes per rate and
byte of input (measured, macOS, containers of 9 * rate elements:
25 bytes per input byte at rate 1, 81 at 4, 312 at 16, 1226 at 64, 5493
at 256) plus about 33 MB for the base. A 3.12.0 row of N values has a
header of b bytes (5 up to 255, 6 up to 32767, 8 above), so a table is
read completely if N <= rate * b, and otherwise up to
(1048576 + h * rate, h = outer header: 6, 7 or 9 bytes) / (N - rate * b) rows; 1100 rows of 1000 nulls need
a rate of 8. The new page of the macro documents the formulas, the
measurements, and two examples that are run by the documentation checks.

The tests of the budget move to tests/src/unit-ubjson_valueless.cpp, which
derives every boundary from the macro and is built with the rates 1,
1000000 and 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF in addition to the default (the last two
check that nothing is refused and that the limit does not wrap around);
they fail with the unchanged header for rate 1, 1000000 and the maximum.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Charge an announced array only what is reserved for it

An array that announced more than reserve_cap() elements but no more than

author: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
message:
A BON8 string ends at the first byte that cannot continue it. When a
string ends a value and is not terminated by 0xFF, that byte belongs to
whatever follows the value, but the reader has already taken it from the
input and keeps it in its push-back buffer. With strict = true the
end-of-input check reports it; with strict = false the buffer was
discarded, so a following value in a stream lost its first byte or bytes
without an error ({0x61, 0x90} read "a" and then dropped the 0 that
follows).

Report parse_error.110 "string at the end of the value is not terminated
by 0xFF" when the push-back buffer is not empty once a BON8 value is
complete and strict is false, as bon8.md requires the final 0xFF. Output
of to_bon8 always has it, so canonical input is not affected.

Fixes #6110.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
subject: Report a missing 0xFF after a final BON8 string also without strict (#6119)

author: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
message:
The seven serializer helpers marked JSON_HEDLEY_ALWAYS_INLINE are inlined
at -O0 as well, and GCC and Clang give every inlined copy its own stack
slots there. That made the recursive frame of dump_container() 2304 bytes
with Clang 21 (2048 with GCC 16), against 480 bytes in 3.12.0, so dump()
of a value nested beyond the default recursion depth limit needed 288 KiB
of stack in an unoptimized build and crashed in a 128 KiB musl thread.

Define JSON_INTERNAL_SERIALIZER_INLINE as JSON_HEDLEY_ALWAYS_INLINE when
__OPTIMIZE__ (or _MSC_VER) is defined and as plain inline otherwise, and
use it for these helpers. The frame drops to 320 bytes and dump() needs
48 KiB at the default limit. The -O2 object code is unchanged with Clang 21
and GCC 16.

Update the stack tables in json_recursion_depth_limit.md and
untrusted_input.md: copying and conversion are now the most demanding
operations at -O0.

Fixes #6116.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
subject: Force inlining of the serializer helpers only in optimized builds (#6117)

message:
* Read a std::u8string from a JSON string and store it as one in every configuration

In C++20, json(std::u8string) was stored as a JSON string only when
std::filesystem::path support was available (the to_json overload sat
inside the JSON_HAS_FILESYSTEM guard), and there was no matching
from_json, so get<std::u8string>() threw type_error.302 ("type must be
array, but is string"). Without std::filesystem, the same expression
still produced an array of code units (the 3.12.0 behavior).

Move the to_json overload out of the filesystem guard so that a
std::u8string is a string in every configuration, build the value
directly from the code units (this also works for a custom string_t
such as the tests' alt_string), and add a from_json overload that reads
a JSON string. The array of numbers written by 3.12.0 is still accepted;
other types throw type_error.302 ("type must be string or array").
std::u8string_view and char8_t arrays are unchanged.

The tests now run in C++20/23 (the file mentions JSON_HAS_CPP_20/23),
also without std::filesystem (test-conversions2_no_filesystem), and with
ordered_json and a custom string type. The new behavior is documented.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Fill the std::u8string with resize and indexing instead of push_back

The push_back loop is not vectorized: reading a 1 kB string took about
2.2 us against 0.39 us with resize and direct element access (clang -O2).

author: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
message:
* docs: state that NaN ordering inside containers depends on the standard

When the element-wise comparison of arrays or objects reaches a NaN and
a number (or another NaN) before any other difference, the result
depends on the language standard. Before C++20 the pair counts as
equivalent and the following elements (or the sizes) decide, so
[1] <= [NaN] is true. Since C++20 the comparison is unordered and
<, <=, >, >= all yield false. Document this on operator<, <=, >, >=
and <=>.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* docs: fix the FILE* notes of parse() and the locking promise

The performance note of parse() said a FILE* is read one character at a
time. With glibc and the Apple C library the characters in the FILE's
buffer are scanned in bulk; only elsewhere is it one character at a
time. The file is locked once only where the C library has unlocked
stdio functions (not on musl, MinGW, newlib, with
JSON_DISABLE_UNLOCKED_FILE_IO, or under MSan). Qualify the promise on
parse.md, sax_parse.md, the parsing page and the performance page.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* docs: fix integer ranges in the MessagePack and BJData tables

number_integer_t is std::int64_t, so number_integer cannot hold values
above 9223372036854775807; those are number_unsigned. The MessagePack
row for uint 64 listed the range up to 18446744073709551615, and the
BJData table had a uint64 row for number_integer that can never be
selected. The CBOR table was already corrected.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* docs: name the macros that turn off FILE* locking and bulk scans

parse() and sax_parse() now say that the FILE* is locked unless
JSON_DISABLE_UNLOCKED_FILE_IO is defined to 1, and the input-source
table and the performance page name JSON_DISABLE_STREAM_BULK_SCAN and
JSON_DISABLE_UNLOCKED_FILE_IO with what each turns off.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

---------

message:
Two views compared equal when the tokens of two floats were equal, and
the same node was equal to itself. An edit writes a NaN as the token
"nan", so a view of it (or of an array holding it) was equal to itself
and to another NaN, while json(NaN) == json(NaN) and view == json are
false. The token shortcut now excludes the edited "nan" token (found by
the missing digit layout), dispatched on the document mode by a tag: a
read-only document cannot hold a NaN, and its walk is unchanged
(instruction count and cycles on canada, citm and twitter within
noise). For editable documents the check costs about 2 % instructions
on canada (cycles within noise). The same-node shortcut is kept for
read-only documents and for editable ones that were never edited; a
document with edits is walked, so comparing it with itself is linear
instead of constant.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
subject: Do not compare an edited NaN equal to itself in json_view (#6085)

author: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
message:
* Document that read() must not be given a view of the document itself

basic_json_document::read() releases the previous text, the decoded
strings and the edits before it parses its input. An input that points
into them (source(), get_string(), number_token(), or a string of an
edited document) is read after its memory was cleared or freed.

A guard that copies such input costs about 1 ns per read() (5 % of a
read of a 7-byte input), which this API exists to avoid, so state the
precondition in read.md, lifetime.md and the pages of the views that
hand out such strings instead, and show how to copy the string first.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Assert in debug builds that read() is not given its own text

read() releases the document's text, decoded strings, owned image and
edits before it parses, so an input that points into them is read after
release. Without NDEBUG, read() now asserts that a borrowed input, a
copied contiguous input and (before C++17) a string_ref input are not
held by the document: its owned text, its decoded strings, an owned
image, and the current buffer of edited strings. Release builds keep
the documented precondition without a check, which would cost 2-4.5 %
per read() of a small message.

JSON_ASSERT is undefined at the end of json.hpp, so the view uses
assert() through a new internal NLOHMANN_VIEW_ASSERT.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

author: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
message:
* Read iterator pairs of std::string and std::vector as pointer ranges

Before C++20, a pair of iterators of a contiguous container cannot be told
from any other random-access iterator, so json::parse(s.begin(), s.end())
on a std::string or std::vector<char> was read one character at a time,
without the bulk scans of strings, numbers and indentation that the
container itself gets (the container overload of input_adapter() already
maps it to a pointer range). The iterators of std::string and of a
std::vector of 1-byte integral elements are now matched exactly and mapped
to the pointer range they cover; an empty range is not dereferenced. The
character type stays the same, so the results and error positions do not
change.

parse(first, last) of a std::string gets 1.7-2.0x as fast in C++17 on an
Apple M1 Max, accept(first, last) 2.7-3.1x, and from_cbor(first, last) of a
std::vector 8-23% faster.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Fix CI: clang-tidy, unused result, Infer false positive in tests

  iterator pair as a false positive

* SWAR: test for special bytes in the reduced form

The usual test for a zero byte, (x - ones) & ~x & high, needs `& ~x` only
to keep bytes from 0x80 out. The tests for quotes, backslashes and control
characters in string_scan.hpp and the serializer also flag every byte from
0x80 with `v & high`, so the `& ~x` terms can be dropped. Clang finds this
reduction itself; GCC does not and emits 24 instead of 16 instructions.

The masks are the same for 1.3 billion random words and for every pair of
adjacent byte values. With GCC 15 on x86-64: accept() -2 to -4 %,
sax_parse() -2 %, dump() -3 %. Clang is unchanged.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Vector scans: one compare for the quote and the control characters

The SSE2/NEON tests for the bytes a string run stops at compared with the
quote, with the backslash and with 0x20 separately. Flipping bit 1 maps
0x00-0x1F onto itself and the quote onto 0x20, and every other ASCII byte
to 33 or more, so (c ^ 2) < 33 finds the quote and the control characters
with one compare: signed where the bytes from 0x80 stop the run too,
unsigned (or with a saturating subtraction / minimum on SSE2) where they
do not. This saves one vector operation per 16 bytes in all twelve vector
tests: the lexer's vector_plain_run() and vector_utf8_run(), dump()'s
copy_plain_halves() and copy_plain_vectors(), and json_view's scanner and
serializer. The DEL tests of the ensure_ascii paths stay.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Tests: sweep_allocator::construct() accepts pointers to const

Recent libc++ (emsdk latest) probes construct(const T*, const T&) in an
unevaluated context while checking for trivial copies; the static_cast to
void* in the noexcept specification then fails to compile.

author: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
message:
dump() batches float tokens of 16 or 17 digits with at least 8 fraction
digits. A damaged image loaded with image_check::bounds can record a
token with no digit before the point and 17 after it, which no JSON
number has. Its q = -17 is outside the range of locate_token(), which
then read fives[17] past its 17 entries; on x86-64 the resulting digits
had 18 digits and failed the assertion of write_decimal() (OSS-Fuzz
issue 583898810, json_view_image_fuzzer).

The batch now takes 8 to 16 fraction digits, which every valid token of
16 or 17 digits has, so it batches the same tokens of valid documents.

author: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
hunk_contexts: JSON_HEDLEY_ALWAYS_INLINE std::size_t accumulate_digits(const char* data, std::s
message:
* Parse JSON in one block of memory with a fused pointer-based parser

The parser and the lexer exchange one token at a time, and the lexer keeps
its state (the current character, a pending unget, where the token starts)
in members, which every character pays for: json::accept() of twitter.json
took 2.8x as long as json_document::accept(). detail::contiguous_parser
reads text in one block of memory through a local pointer, with the
grammar, the whitespace and the tokens in one loop (after yyjson's reader),
and drives a SAX handler: parse()'s DOM handler, accept()'s handler, or the
user's handler of sax_parse(). It is used with the default options (no
callback, no comments, no trailing commas; sax_parse() with strict = true).

Errors are reported by the library parser, so the exception, its message and
its position stay the same. contiguous_parser stops at the token that the
library parser would reject, before reporting it, so the events up to the
error are the same; then:
- parse() runs the library parser with a handler that only reports the
  error (json_sax_error_reporter), with the lexer of parse(), which is
  instantiated anyway;
- sax_parse() runs it with a handler that forwards only parse_error() to
  the user's handler (json_sax_error_forwarder), so no event arrives twice;
- accept() returns the verdict.
A handler that returns false stops the parse as before. An error at the end
of a large input costs parse() about 1.2x of what it cost before.

On an Apple M1 Max: accept() 1.6-2.0x as fast, parse() 10-16% faster,
ordered_json 11-16%, sax_parse() with a user's handler 1.36-1.46x, small
messages 12-22% (parse()) and 2.1-2.4x (accept()). On x86-64 (GCC 15,
Clang 21): accept() 1.6-1.9x, parse() 5-17%, ordered_json 12-19%,
sax_parse() 1.32-1.57x. A translation unit that parses a string compiles 3%
(-O0) and 9% (-O2) slower.

unit-contiguous_parser.cpp compares the contiguous path with the byte path
(std::list iterators) on corner cases, generated documents, their
truncations and mutations, deep nesting, and narrow number types: the same
values with the same number types and float bits, exception messages,
accept() verdicts and sax_parse() events.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Fix CI: unused parameter without exceptions, cpplint, BUILD.bazel

- json_sax_error_reporter::parse_error: mark the exception unused, as
  JSON_THROW does not use it with JSON_NOEXCEPTION
- unit-contiguous_parser.cpp: compare the exceptions of both paths only
  when exceptions are enabled (invalid input aborted the test otherwise)
- silence cpplint's readability/braces false positives on the if
  statements inside the parser's macros
- add contiguous_parser.hpp to BUILD.bazel

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* accept(): skip digits without computing their value

accept() needs the value of a number only for a float whose exponent may
reach the largest value. skip_digits() finds the end of the digits without
the multiply-adds of accumulate_digits(), and once an 8-byte word fails the
digit test, the remaining loop needs no bounds check: a non-digit is in
that word. The value is computed afterwards for the rare floats that need
it.

accept() of canada.json: -16 % on Apple M1, -22 % with GCC 15 and -21 %
with Clang 21 on x86-64; files with many numbers -9 to -15 %.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Tests: mark parser callback in unit-contiguous_parser noexcept

Fixes the -Werror=noexcept failure with GCC 26 (ci_test_standards_gcc (26)).

author: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
message:
#5835 replaced the switch on the value type in operator*, operator->,
operator++, operator-- and operator== of iter_impl with an if chain that
tests for an array first. Every step over an object then pays for a
failed test and a taken branch: with the iterator inlined, walking
twitter.json took 14% more cycles than with 3.12.0, and citm_catalog.json
3.5% more.

Test for objects first. Walking every value of the three files now
takes fewer cycles than with 3.12.0 (Apple M1 Max, Apple clang 21):
citm_catalog.json 1.21x, twitter.json 1.04x, canada.json 1.17x as fast.

A post for the documentation (Home > Blog) on how 3.13.0 became faster:
eight themes with the pull requests behind them, the ideas taken from other
libraries, what did not work, how the fast paths are tested, and the
compile-time cost. Every number comes from a run on 2026-10-27 (3.12.0 against
develop plus the open non-draft PRs, Apple M1 Max) or from the linked PR.

  inline SVGs in the nj-charts style; data/perf_timeline.csv holds the
  timeline.
- tests/benchmarks/history: history.cpp and history.py time one fixed program
  against the header of every commit that changed it, interleaved, and write
  one CSV row per commit with its PR. The timeline of the post comes from it.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* docs: compare json_document with Glaze, sonic, RapidJSON and Rust parsers

Extends the comparison in "How 3.13.0 got faster" from yyjson, simdjson and
Boost.JSON to eleven engines: sonic-cpp, RapidJSON and Glaze (generic DOM,
lazy_json, reading into structs) in C++, sonic-rs, simd-json and serde_json in

Haswell server (GCC 13, Clang 18). Every engine must return the same values,
string bytes and bit-identical number sums before it is timed.

The post now answers whether json_document is the fastest parser: it is the
fastest document parser at parse+dump everywhere and at parsing on Apple
silicon, ties with simdjson's DOM on x86-64, and loses to simdjson On-Demand
and Glaze structs when only a few fields are read.

crate with its Cargo.lock), summarize.py and the pinned versions and checksums.

author: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
message:
* Scan the buffer of a FILE in bulk with glibc and the Apple C library

Parsing from a FILE* still read one character at a time through
getc_unlocked(), while a std::istream has its get area scanned in bulk.
file_input_adapter now offers the lexer the same kind of window into the
buffer of the FILE: it reads the fields that the C library's own
getc_unlocked() macro reads (glibc: _IO_read_ptr and _IO_read_end; Apple:
_p and _r) and consumes exactly the characters getc_unlocked() would
return, so the file is left where it was left before. The part of the
current token in a buffer that is about to be refilled is kept for error
messages, as for streams. The window needs the file locked for the whole
parse, so JSON_DISABLE_UNLOCKED_FILE_IO and MemorySanitizer builds turn it
off; uClibc, which defines __GLIBC__ but has other fields, does not get it.

parse() from a FILE* gets 2.0-2.6x as fast on an Apple M1 Max and 1.7-2.2x
on x86-64 (glibc, GCC 15 and Clang 21), accept() 2.9-4.4x; that is about as
fast as parsing from a std::ifstream. The new tests read with FILE buffers
of 1 to 70 bytes and unbuffered files, after ungetc(), with SAX positions
and with binary strings across the buffer's edges.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Tests: no setvbuf() buffer below 2 bytes on Windows

The Microsoft C runtime rejects a _IOFBF buffer size below 2 as an
invalid parameter and ends the process (0xc0000409), which made
test-file_input fail on all MSVC and clang-cl jobs.

message:
* Binary readers: append strings straight from contiguous input

get_bytes() read every string into a zero-filled resize() and copied the
bytes over it, so each byte was written twice. A string that the input holds
in one block (bulk_remaining() at least its length) is now appended from it
directly. The claimed length is checked against the input first, so a huge
claimed length still allocates nothing it cannot fill; other inputs and
binary values keep the chunked loop.

5.5-9.1% faster on an Apple M1 Max and 2.7-8.6% on x86-64 (GCC 15, Clang 21);
canada.json, which has few strings, is unchanged.

author: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
message:
* Binary reader and writer: remove checks that invariants make dead

Branch coverage of the test suite and of 24k mutated inputs showed
these conditions as never taken; each is implied by a check made
earlier on the same path:

- check_bson_document_size: `document_size < 0` (the size was rejected
  below 5 before it was stored)
- get_ubjson_ndarray_size: `second != 'N'` ('N' is rejected as a type
  marker before `second` can be set)
- bjd_type_name() == nullptr for an ndarray dtype: every marker
  is_valid_optimized_type() accepts for BJData has a name (now an assert)
- the early is_bjd_excluded_optimized_type() check in
  get_ubjson_size_type(): is_valid_optimized_type() rejects the same
  eight markers with the same error
- `input_format == bjdata` next to `is_ndarray`, bit 8 of the type, or a
  'B'/'u'/'m'/'M' marker: these only arise for BJData
- `first != npos` next to bit 8: the bit is only set after a count
- MessagePack writer: the `<= max` halves of the negative int8/16/32
  ladder (the ladder is in the `else` of `n >= 0`)

No change in behaviour: a build that aborts on each removed side passes
the test suite and the fuzz corpora, and a 1.6M-input differential run
of the reader against the original headers found no difference.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Remove is_bjd_excluded_optimized_type(), which has no caller left; fix two comments

is_valid_optimized_type() rejects the markers BJData excludes, so the reader
no longer needs its own list; the test now checks is_valid_optimized_type()

author: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
message:
output_vector_sink grew the vector by resizing it to its whole new
capacity. resize() zeroes the characters it adds, so every doubling
zeroed megabytes of a fresh allocation at once: that faults in all its
pages and evicts them from the cache before the writer reaches them,
and the writer's stores then miss again. The sink now reserves the same
capacity as before but resizes the vector only to 64 KiB
(vector_sink_window) ahead of the position, which is still cached when
the writer's stores come.

to_cbor(), to_msgpack(), to_ubjson(), to_bjdata() and to_bon8() of an
array of one million numbers into a fresh vector: 4-26 % faster on x86
(Skylake laptop with Apple clang 13, Haswell VPS with GCC 16 and
Clang 23), 1-2.5 % on Apple M1 Max; other documents unchanged (within
0.4 % in reruns). The capacity and growth of the vector are as before.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
subject: Binary writers: zero only a window ahead of the vector sink's position (#6020)

author: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
message:
* UBJSON/BJData reader: reject a container count equal to SIZE_MAX

The reader marks a container whose count is not known by npos, which
is SIZE_MAX. A count of exactly that value was stored unchanged and
then read as "no count", so the BJData input

    [ # M ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff i 01 ]

parsed as [1] instead of throwing out_of_range.408 as a count of
2^64-2 does. Where size_t is 32 bits, the same holds for 'm' and 'L'
counts of 2^32-1, in UBJSON too.

The counts of 'm', 'M' and the signed types now go through
store_ubjson_count(), which rejects npos with "integer value overflow"
(the message a count beyond size_t already gets), as the CBOR reader
does in get_cbor_container_size(). An ND-array dimension of 2^64-1 gets
the same message now, where it was "excessive ndarray size caused
overflow" (the product check) on 64-bit platforms.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* MessagePack reader: reject an array/map 32 length equal to SIZE_MAX

On a platform with a 32-bit std::size_t, an array 32 or map 32 length of
0xFFFFFFFF equals unknown_size(), so start_array()/start_object() were
told the size was unknown and skipped the max_size() check. Route both
through the CBOR length check, renamed get_container_size(), which
already rejects that value.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

author: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
message:
enter_cbor_array and enter_msgpack_array called the out-of-line scalar
run for every non-empty array. When the array's element is an object or
an array, as on every level of [[...]] or the single ring of a GeoJSON
polygon, the call reads nothing; it made 1,000 arrays nested in each
other cost 4 % more instructions (GCC 13) and up to 8 % more time (Apple
clang) than without the run. #5975 had fixed that with an inline
pre-check, which was later dropped after measuring canada only.

The run is now entered only for arrays of two or more elements: the same
comparison as before, so no other row changes. Arrays of one scalar,
which the run read faster, now take the general path; they are rare in
documents (one in citm_catalog, none in twitter or canada). The new
benchmark FromBinaryShape/singles measures them, next to
FromBinaryShape/nested.

Instructions per repetition, new/old, GCC 13 callgrind: nested arrays
0.973 (CBOR) and 0.971 (MessagePack), arrays of one scalar 1.037 and
1.021, every other row within 0.15 %.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
subject: CBOR/MessagePack readers: leave one-element arrays to the general path (#6008)

author: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
message:
* Create the DOM parser's member value before placing it (#5985)

json_sax_dom_parser::set_member() constructed the new value in place over
the null member. basic_json(value_t) sets the type before the json_value
allocates, so a std::bad_alloc left a member typed object/array with a
null pointer, and the destructor crashed instead of propagating the
exception. Construct the value first and move it over the member (the
move constructor is noexcept).

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Fix CI for the parse() bad_alloc sweep test (#5985)

- sweep_allocator: provide max_size(), construct() and destroy(), which
  GCC 4.8's std::map calls on the allocator directly.
- Declare the non-throwing test lambdas noexcept (-Werror=noexcept on
  recent GCC).
- Give the sax_parse lambda an explicit return type; Clang 3.4 crashes on
  the deduced one in C++11 mode.
- Skip the parser callback sweep with iterator debugging (MSVC debug
  builds, clang-cl), where containers allocate debug proxies inside
  noexcept move constructors and terminate instead of throwing, as in the
  other allocator tests.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01N5NasAgbDGG28MqXjQvLqp
Signed-off-by: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Construct a scalar member in place; only a throwing value goes through a temporary

Creating the value first and moving it over the member is needed only when
creating it can throw (a string, a binary value or a container). A scalar
or null is again constructed in place, without the extra move and destroy
per member (and, with JSON_DIAGNOSTICS, without the extra set_parents()).

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Spell the nothrow trait without && and fix the construct_member comments

The dispatch in set_member tests std::is_nothrow_constructible, not
whether the value is a scalar. Say so in the comments, and drop the &&
from the trait argument (equivalent for a forwarding reference) so that
astyle no longer inserts spaces around the template brackets.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Say "for example" in the construct_member comments

The overloads are selected by std::is_nothrow_constructible, not by the
kind of value: a custom type that cannot throw takes the first one.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

author: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
message:
* basic_json, iterators, serializer: remove checks that invariants make dead

Branch coverage of the test suite and of 24k mutated inputs showed
these conditions as never taken; each is implied by the code around it:

- copy_object_level(): `src_it != src_object.cend()`; dst was built from
  exactly src_object.size() unique keys and src_it advances at most once
  per member
- the general comparison operators (equal_general, less_general,
  three_way_general): the five same-type scalar cases, which the inline
  fast path of every operator handles before calling them (now an
  assert); and the NaN half of compares_unordered() in the mixed-type
  branch, reached only after all six number pairs returned, where only
  a discarded operand is unordered
- serializer, ensure_ascii: the reset of `bytes` under error_handler_t::keep
  and the surrogate-pair escape in the UTF8_ACCEPT case; every
  well-formed multi-byte character is escaped by write_u_escapes() before
  decode() sees it, so decode() only ever accepts DEL here, a single byte
  of which nothing was buffered (now asserts)
- iter_impl(pointer): the if/else chain assigned value-initialized
  iterators to the value-initialized m_it

No change in behaviour: a build that aborts on each removed side passes
the test suite, the fuzz corpora and 23.2M dumps of all 1-, 2- and
boundary 4-byte strings in both ensure_ascii modes.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* iter_impl: keep the type-dependent initialization in the constructor

The check is not needed for correctness (m_it is value-initialized), but
without it GCC 13 generates slower iteration loops: a recursive walk over
a parsed document takes 0.5-2.7 % longer (callgrind: +1.9 % instructions
on twitter.json, +0.95 % on canada.json). Clang generates identical code
either way. See the measurements in #6005.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

---------

message:

- lexer: `next_unget` in get_codepoint_bulk() and scan_literal_bulk().

  and in skip_bom(); every token scan starts with a plain get() in

message:
* CI: measure line coverage without lcov's unexecuted-block adjustment

Drop geninfo_unexecuted_blocks=1 from the lcov capture of ci_test_coverage:
it reset every line of an inlined or templated function to 0 as soon as one
copy had an unexecuted block, which understated the line coverage by about
three points.

Add -fvar-tracking-assignments to both coverage builds. At -O0, GCC inlines
always_inline functions before it places the coverage counters, so the call
sites of such helpers (put_literal() and others) got no line record and
showed as 0 in an -O3 translation unit that never reaches them. With the
flag, the call sites carry counts in every translation unit. The generated
code is identical.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Remove unreachable code found by the coverage analysis

Remove code that no input can reach, and mark the lines that cannot be
covered with LCOV_EXCL_LINE:

- BJData writer: the dry_run parameter of the ND-array element writers was
  always true; replace them by range checks.
- BON8 writer: call throw_integer_out_of_range() directly instead of
  write_bon8_value() for values that always throw.
- binary_writer: integer_bits() is only called for integers of up to 64 bits.
- serializer, view serializer, lexer: replace guards that the callers make
  unreachable by assertions or by the simpler code (surrogate pairs under
  ensure_ascii, next_unget, '-' at the end of the buffer).
- json_view: drop unreachable branches in scalar(), set(), check_utf8_scan(),
  append_input_impl() and unescape().
- Mark exception-cleanup braces, 2 GiB limits, big-endian and 32-bit code, and
  fall-through case labels with LCOV_EXCL_LINE.

No behavior changes for any input that reaches these functions.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Tests: cover the remaining lines of the library headers

Add tests for the lines of include/nlohmann that were not covered: the
binary readers and writers, the lexer and locale paths, the json_view
modules, the custom number, key and array types, json_pointer, json_patch,
diff and the iterators.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Fix test failures in the coverage tests

- unit-custom-object-key-type: remove the unused make_strict_key(strict_key)
  overload, the unused range constructor and default constructor, and guard
  data() with JSON_DIAGNOSTICS (unused-function/-member-function errors with
  GCC and clang -Weverything).
- unit-json_view_compare: move the two new sections to the new
  unit-json_view_compare_values.cpp, as the object file got too large for the
  MinGW assembler again, and use a std::map with std::greater instead of
  std::unordered_map, which does not accept the incomplete basic_json
  (clang 3.9, icpc).
- unit-json_view_dump: rename the variables that hid outer ones (MSVC C4456).
- unit-stream-bulk-scan: restore the real size of the oversized get area
  before the adapter is destroyed (JSON_PRECISE_STREAM_POSITION reads the
  character at the read position), and skip the test where the streambuf
  cannot hold a get area larger than an int (MSVC).
- unit-regression1: with JSON_NO_THREAD_LOCAL, copies are built member by
  member and keep correct timestamps, so check the corresponding outcome.

* Keep the byte range in exceptions about the root value (#5987)

With JSON_DIAGNOSTICS and JSON_DIAGNOSTIC_POSITIONS both set, exception::diagnostics()

for a null value, the same change as #6003, so either can be merged first.

In the view, a value that value_path() does not find leaves no tokens, so the
found flag added nothing to the tokens.empty() test.

author: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
message:
* Make basic_json::insert() provide its documented strong exception guarantee (#5986)

A failed allocation while the new elements were copied left the value
changed, and with JSON_DIAGNOSTICS stale parent pointers behind. The
extra work now happens almost only on the failure path:

- Array insert(pos, cnt, val) and insert(pos, first, last) append the
  copies at the end and rotate them into place. If a copy throws, the
  appended elements are erased again (noexcept) and the parents are set.
  Moving a basic_json cannot throw, so reallocation is safe. This is no
  slower than vector::insert (faster for numbers), needs no temporary
  array, and keeps the elements that libstdc++ lost on reallocation.
- Array insert(pos, val) copies a non-scalar value first and inserts it
  by move, except at the end, where vector::insert is strong. Scalars
  keep the direct path.
- The object range insert(first, last) into an empty object uses the
  container's own range insertion and clears the object on an exception.
  Into a non-empty object it inserts member by member and logs one bit
  per source member (a new member is detected by the size change; no
  allocation for the first 256 members); on an exception the members
  added are erased by walking the source range. No assumption that
  key_type is string_t.
- The parents are set when a failed insertion is undone.

The regression test fails every allocation of every insert() overload in
turn, for json and ordered_json, and checks the value and its parents.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Fix clang-tidy and -Wnrvo findings in insert rollback helpers

Declare the rollback helpers non-movable, replace the nested conditional
and C array in object_insert_rollback, silence the intentional copy in the
allocator test, and avoid the missed NRVO in the test factory lambda.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01N5NasAgbDGG28MqXjQvLqp
Signed-off-by: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>

* insert(): strong guarantee for single elements, basic for the rest

Rework of the previous two commits, following the discussion in #5996:
the standard containers give the strong guarantee only for a single
element (std::vector: at the end, or if the exception does not come from
copying T; std::map: single-element insert), and copying a basic_json
allocates. Rebuilding a rollback for the count, range and object-range
overloads on top of array_t/object_t made the code verbose and slower.

- insert(pos, const basic_json&): at end() forward as before (the
  standard covers it); elsewhere copy first and insert by move, as
  libstdc++ does internally (libc++ shifts the tail before copying).
- insert_iterator() and object insert(first, last) set the parents in a
  scope guard, so a failed insertion leaves a valid value with
  JSON_DIAGNOSTICS too (the next assert_invariant() aborted before).
- Docs: strong guarantee for (1), basic guarantee for (2)-(5); the
  argument checks throw before anything is changed.
- Test: allocation-failure sweep checks the strong guarantee for (1) and
  validity, type and parents for the other overloads.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* insert(): document the exception safety of overloads 2 to 5 once

The four basic-guarantee statements were identical up to array/object.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* insert(): simplify the wording of the basic guarantee

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

author: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
message:
* Do not construct the base class when destroying a container (#5995)

json_value::destroy_container() and destroy_walk() used default-
constructed basic_json values as stand-ins, which construct a
CustomBaseClass that belongs to no value. A base class whose default
constructor allocates made the noexcept destructor allocate again, and
terminate if that allocation failed, which #5762 set out to prevent.

Use data (type and value, no base class) as the stand-in instead, and
pass the children's m_data to the walk helpers.

Add a test with a counting base class: destroying a value constructs no
base object and destroys exactly one per value, also for values nested
deeper than the recursion depth limit.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Release the test value with = nullptr instead of reset()

clang-tidy (readability-ambiguous-smartptr-reset-call) rejects j.reset()
because the pointee inherits a reset() from counting_base.

message:
* UBJSON/BJData readers: read optimized arrays of numbers in one loop

An array with a type marker for a fixed-size number ($U, $i, $I, $l, $L,
$d, $D, and BJData's $u, $m, $M), including the data of a BJData ndarray,

elements that are in the input in one loop - load, byte swap for the

input ends before, other types, and non-contiguous inputs are read as

GCC reports -Werror=unused-result for static_cast<void>(json::from_ubjson(...))
and json::from_bjdata(...): a cast to void does not silence warn_unused_result

author: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
message:
* MessagePack reader: read runs of scalar array elements in one loop

As for CBOR: when an array opens and the input is contiguous, read the
integers, floats, booleans, and nils that follow in a tight loop instead
of going through parse_msgpack_internal and parse_msgpack_value for every
element. The loop stops at any other kind of value and when fewer than 9
bytes are left; those values are read by the general path as before.
Non-contiguous inputs are not affected.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* MessagePack reader: enter the scalar run only when a scalar follows

As for CBOR: enter_msgpack_array tests the first byte and the remaining length
inline and calls the out-of-line run only for a scalar, so arrays of maps or
strings no longer pay for a call that reads nothing; the run's loop condition
moves to the end (do-while).

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* MessagePack reader: mark the initial accepted in the scalar run as a false-positive dead store

ci_infer reports DEAD_STORE for 'bool accepted = true;' in the MessagePack
scalar run, as in the CBOR one, because every case assigns accepted before it
is read.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* MessagePack tests: assign the parsed value instead of casting it to void

GCC (ci_test_gcc) reports -Werror=unused-result for
static_cast<void>(json::from_msgpack(...)): a cast to void does not silence
warn_unused_result on GCC. Assign to a json, as the other tests in the file do.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* MessagePack reader: drop the scalar pre-check before the run

enter_msgpack_array now calls the run directly, and parse_msgpack_scalar_run
tests the remaining count and length at the top of a while loop instead of
relying on msgpack_scalar_follows(); its own switch already leaves on any
value that is not a scalar.

Instructions per repetition, new/old: SAX canada 0.946 (clang) and 0.973
(GCC 13), DOM read canada 0.991 / 0.992; no row more than 0.3 % higher.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* MessagePack reader: say why the initial accepted in the scalar run stays

As for CBOR: Infer's DEAD_STORE report is right, not a false positive. The
initializer is kept for clang-tidy's cppcoreguidelines-init-variables.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* MessagePack reader: give the scalar run the bulk tag instead of a wrapper

As for CBOR: parse_msgpack_scalar_run takes the bulk-scan tag itself and is
the function kept out of line, so parse_msgpack_array_start goes.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* MessagePack reader: start the scalar run's accepted at false

As for CBOR: Infer ignores dead stores of 0, so the suppression goes.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* MessagePack reader: let the scalar run find its array itself

As for CBOR: parse_msgpack_scalar_run reads container_stack.back() in its
bulk version, so the caller no longer evaluates it for input that is not
contiguous.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

author: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
message:
* Binary readers: swap the bytes of floats with a single byteswap

byte_swap reversed float and double values byte by byte. GCC does not
merge that loop into one bswap, and C++23's std::byteswap accepts only
integers. Overloads for float and double now copy the bits into a
uint32_t/uint64_t, call detail::byteswap, and copy them back. This
applies to every binary reader that uses get_number.

In the CBOR reader, the single- and double-precision float cases call a
non-inlined helper. Without it, GCC stopped inlining the stream
adapter's get_character() into parse_cbor_internal, which made reading
from a std::istream about 0.5 % slower.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* CBOR reader: inline get_cbor_float() and always inline get() instead

The never-inlined get_cbor_float() costs a call for every float read
from input without bulk access: reading canada.json from CBOR through a
FILE* became 5.6 % slower on Apple clang in the benchmark suite. The
helper existed only because GCC 13 stopped inlining the stream adapter's
get_character() into parse_cbor_internal. Always inlining
binary_reader::get() fixes that as well.

callgrind, all binary formats on buffer, std::istringstream and FILE*
input (canada and citm_catalog): GCC 13 0.986-1.003, GCC 16 0.994-1.006,
Clang 23 identical. Apple clang suite: FromBinaryFile/cbor/canada 0.939,
geomean of the 53 binary reader rows 0.998.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

---------

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
subject: Binary readers: swap the bytes of floats with a single byteswap (#5976)

author: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
message:
* CBOR reader: read runs of scalar array elements in one loop

When a definite-length CBOR array opens and the input is contiguous, read
the integers, floats, booleans, and nulls that follow in a tight loop
instead of going through parse_cbor_internal's container logic and
parse_cbor_value's dispatch for every element. The loop stops at any other
kind of value and when fewer than 9 bytes are left; those values are read
by the general path exactly as before. Non-contiguous inputs are not
affected (tag dispatch on the bulk-scan capability).

Also pass a member empty string as the number source to number_float
instead of constructing a std::string for every float.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* CBOR reader: address review of the scalar-run reader

- parse_cbor_scalar_run: set the size explicitly in every case that
  reads a value, instead of relying on a default that every other case
  overwrites.
- Remove cbor_scalar_follows(): parse_cbor_scalar_run already returns on
  the same conditions, and without the pre-check SAX canada needs another
  8.5 % fewer instructions with GCC 13 (0.915 against the previous
  version), with no row more than 0.5 % worse (Mac and GCC).
- Restore the comment on why parse_cbor_internal copies the container
  frame.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* CBOR reader: enter the scalar run only when a scalar follows

An array of containers or strings called the out-of-line run start once per
array only to leave it at once; on nested data (arrays of objects) that call
made reading slower than before the run reader. enter_cbor_array now tests the
first byte and the remaining length inline and calls the run only for a
scalar, so the run's loop condition moves to the end (do-while).

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* CBOR reader: mark the initial accepted in the scalar run as a false-positive dead store

ci_infer reports DEAD_STORE for 'bool accepted = true;' in
parse_cbor_scalar_run because every case assigns accepted before it is read.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* CBOR reader: drop the scalar pre-check before the run

enter_cbor_array calls the run directly again, and parse_cbor_scalar_run
tests the remaining count and length at the top of a while loop; its own
switch already leaves on any value that is not a scalar. The MessagePack
reader is built the same way.

Instructions per repetition, new/old: clang SAX canada 0.983, read canada
0.993; GCC 13 read canada 0.997, the other rows at most 1.004.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* CBOR reader: say why the initial accepted in the scalar run stays

Infer's DEAD_STORE report is right, not a false positive: every case that
reaches the read assigns accepted. The initializer is kept for clang-tidy's
cppcoreguidelines-init-variables.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* CBOR reader: give the scalar run the bulk tag instead of a wrapper

parse_cbor_scalar_run takes the bulk-scan tag itself and is the function that
is kept out of line, so the one-line parse_cbor_array_start wrapper goes, as
the UBJSON typed run already does.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* CBOR reader: start the scalar run's accepted at false

Infer ignores dead stores of 0 (--liveness-ignored-constant defaults to "0"),
and false is 0 to it, so the suppression and its comment go.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* CBOR reader: let the scalar run find its array itself

parse_cbor_scalar_run reads container_stack.back() in its bulk version, so
the caller no longer evaluates it for input that is not contiguous.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

message:
#5634 made dump() write integers below 10^16 eight digits at a time; larger
ones still took the two-digits-per-division loop and count_digits(). Random
64-bit integers almost all have 17 to 20 digits (99.9 % of signed_ints.json
and unsigned_ints.json), so Dump/signed_ints and Dump/unsigned_ints gained
only 1.4x over 3.12.0, against 2.3x for small integers.

A 64-bit magnitude is now written as its first one to four digits and two
groups of eight. Wider magnitudes (__int128 and class types, #5805) keep the
loop: number types of at most 64 bits are selected by type, so no comparison
is reported as always true; for others the value is compared. The sign
handling of #1447/#5815 (remove_sign() into number_magnitude_t) is unchanged.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
subject: Write integers of 17 to 20 digits eight digits at a time in dump() (#5964)

author: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
message:
A json_view or json_document decodes a macro-defined struct directly and looks
the members up by their decoded keys. Only plain keys were covered so far.

The new section decodes structs defined with NLOHMANN_DEFINE_TYPE_INTRUSIVE,
..._WITH_DEFAULT and ..._WITH_NAMES from documents whose keys contain escape
sequences, and compares the result with the conversion of the materialized
value. It also pins the difference for a duplicate key written once plain and
once escaped (the view takes the first member, the materialized value keeps
the last one), and that an escaped backslash is part of the decoded key.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
subject: Test escaped object keys decoded through NLOHMANN_DEFINE_TYPE from a json_view (#5972)

author: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
message:
After the first \uXXXX escape of a string, slow_string() now decodes the
escapes that follow it directly, while the next six bytes are \u and four hex
digits that are not a surrogate, instead of going round its main loop for each
of them (that is how Python's json.dumps writes non-ASCII text by default).
A surrogate, a bad digit, or fewer than six bytes leave the position at the
backslash: the main loop handles them as before and reports the same error at
the same position.

twitterescaped.json (simdjson-data, 549 KB, 33,036 escapes), json_document::parse(),
A/B in one binary, 6 code layouts, time after / before:

- Apple M1 Max, Apple clang 21: 0.897
- x86-64 Haswell, GCC 16.2: 0.907
- x86-64 Haswell, Clang 23: 0.910

The other files of the benchmark set (twitter, citm_catalog, canada, gsoc-2018,
apache_builds, instruments, tree-pretty, github_events, random, update-center,
semanticscholar-corpus, twitter_timeline) stay within the noise of each machine.

New test: chains of every length from 1 to 40 of escapes that give one, two,
and three bytes of UTF-8, followed by the end of the string, text, escapes,
surrogates, bad digits, and cut in every place, in keys and in values, against
json::parse().

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
subject: json_view: decode chains of unicode escapes in a loop (#5969)

message:
* Compare json_view values without a vector per container and a basic_json per number

operator== of views (view/view, view/json, and editable documents) built two
vectors of members for every object it entered, sorted them with stable_sort
for every object, and converted each number to a basic_json value. It now:

- keeps the members of all open objects in one vector (reserved with
  geometric growth, so that nested objects do not reallocate), and orders
  them by insertion sort for up to 16 members, or not at all when the keys
  ascend already;
- compares numbers of one type directly, and builds a basic_json only for
  numbers of different types;
- compares short texts (keys, numbers, most strings) with two overlapping
  loads (bytes_equal(), in node.hpp);
- first walks both documents in lockstep, in the order of their text, which
  finds most pairs of equal values without the work of the comparison. The
  walk only enters an object if the comparison would visit its members in the
  same order (the object type keeps the order, the keys ascend, or all values
  are scalars), so a difference is never found later than before, and it
  records the containers it found different, so that the comparison does not
  walk them again;
- rejects values of different types and arrays of different sizes before any
  of this, and, for an object type that keeps the order, objects whose first
  (up to four) members have different keys, which ends a comparison that
  differs near the start without preparing the members.

Results are unchanged: numbers compare by value across types, duplicate keys
resolve as parse() resolves them, and objects compare in document order for
ordered_json and by key otherwise.

Instructions of one comparison of a document with an equal copy, macOS arm64
(develop -> now), json_document / ordered_json_document / editable:

  twitter    16.1M -> 7.0M   17.7M -> 1.5M    16.6M -> 7.3M
  citm       45.0M -> 3.4M   47.0M -> 3.2M    45.7M -> 4.3M
  canada    111.4M -> 13.7M  111.4M -> 13.7M  113.3M -> 15.0M
  jeopardy   26.2M -> 3.7M   27.3M -> 3.7M    26.6M -> 12.1M

and of a view with a basic_json value:

  twitter    11.4M -> 5.9M   11.2M -> 7.3M    11.6M -> 5.9M
  citm       33.9M -> 9.7M   32.6M -> 9.1M    34.6M -> 9.8M
  canada     92.9M -> 32.1M  92.9M -> 32.1M   93.9M -> 32.8M

and Linux instruction counts (GCC 13 / Clang 18) of the same comparisons:

  document with an equal copy   json_document     ordered_json_document   editable
    twitter                     -49 % / -52 %     -89 % / -89 %           -48 % / -50 %
    citm                        -90 % / -89 %     -91 % / -90 %           -88 % / -87 %
    jeopardy (4,000 questions)  -85 % / -85 %     -86 % / -86 %           -46 % / -49 %
  view with a basic_json value
    twitter                     -41 % / -45 %     -28 % / -35 %           -45 % / -44 %
    citm                        -63 % / -65 %     -63 % / -66 %           -65 % / -64 %
    jeopardy                    -39 % / -43 %     -14 % / -24 %           -44 % / -43 %

A sweep that places one difference at about 2,100 positions of eight
documents (a token at an even spacing, the first and last tokens, the first,
middle and last member of the root removed, one appended, the document
wrapped) in five kinds of comparison (view/view of read-only and of editable
documents, view/json, json_document, editable/view) finds the same results as
before and no placement slower on the Mac (Clang); on Linux no placement is
slower than 3 % (Clang and GCC).

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Check the float tokens of a json_document image without a sort and a scan of every character

load(image_check::full) checked every float token of an image by sorting
the token ranges, scanning the token character by character, and comparing
the digit layout with the node's. Now:

- the ranges are sorted only if they are not sorted already (save() writes
  them in the order of the nodes, so they are);
- a token of the shape [-]digits.digits whose digit counts are the ones the
  node records (nearly all of them) is accepted by checking its digits eight
  at a time, without the general scan;
- the general scan skips runs of digits eight at a time.

Damaged tokens are still rejected as before: the check accepts exactly the
tokens that the general scan accepts.

Instructions of load(image_check::full) (develop -> now):

  macOS arm64        canada 44.6M -> 30.9M (-31 %), jeopardy 11.3M -> 10.7M,
                     citm 10.4M -> 10.0M, twitter 5.06M -> 4.94M
  Linux GCC 13       canada -50 %, jeopardy -43 %, twitter -31 %, citm -28 %
  Linux Clang 18     canada -42 %, jeopardy -48 %, twitter -35 %, citm -32 %

image_check::bounds is unchanged (within 0.4 %).

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Rename names that Flawfinder takes for the file function open()

The comparison cursors' open() is now enter(), and a test's open and
close strings are head and tail.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Fix the compiler and lint failures of the json_view comparison

- all_digits(): the lambda declares its constant itself; MSVC does not
  let a lambda without captures read a constexpr local of the function
- equal(): the frame's "in document order" index is a namespace-scope
  constant (document_order); the local constexpr npos in the default
  member initializers of the local struct crashed GCC 9 and MinGW GCC
  and was not found by MSVC
- keys_differ_early() keeps the first keys in std::arrays (cpplint:
  variable-length arrays; clang-tidy: C arrays), and the basic_json
  side's first_keys() is not noexcept (key() may throw)
- the numbers of one type are compared in an if chain instead of a
  nested conditional operator
- the dump test avoids C arrays and temporary string concatenations

View comparison instructions are unchanged (Apple clang, twitter, citm,
canada: -0.1 % to +0.1 %).

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Keep the byte comparison helpers in compare.hpp

Address review comments: bytes_equal() and bytes_less() move from node.hpp
to compare.hpp, their only user; key_less() no longer splits the comment of
resolve_indices() from its function; and the loop counters of bytes_equal()
and all_digits() are scoped to their loops.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Dispatch on the compile-time conditions of the json_view comparison

MSVC (/W4 /WX) reported C4127 (conditional expression is constant) for
the template parameter EA and the object type's ordering in an if
condition; both are now tag-dispatched.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Remove a nested duplicate guard from the json_view image test

clang-tidy reported the inner #if !defined(JSON_NOEXCEPTION) as
redundant (the test case is in the same #if) and a find() != npos, which
gets the NOLINT the other tests use.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Mark Infer's null dereference in materialize() as a false positive

Infer (ci_infer, also red on develop since #5882) reports a null
dereference in json_sax_dom_parser::null() called from materialize(). The
member pointer the parser stores a value of an object in is set by the
key() before it, so it is not null there.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Move the json_view comparison tests into their own file

With the tests this branch adds, the object file of unit-json_view_dump.cpp
got too large for the MinGW x64 assembler ("file too big"). The test case
"json_view comparison" is now unit-json_view_compare.cpp, unchanged and
also built with C++17.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Build the DOM parser with Visual Studio 2015 again

Since #5882, the three VS 2015 jobs of AppVeyor fail on develop:
- the detection of keys that can be indexed instantiated std::hash for
  every string type, which VS 2015 rejects with a static_assert for a type
  it does not hash (alt_string): std::hash is now looked at only for
  objects in a vector
- the frame stack copied its frames with std::copy to a raw pointer, which
  VS 2015 reports as unsafe (C4996, an error with /WX): a loop now

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* json_view: no per-object allocations in ordered_json comparisons

For an object type that keeps the order of its members (ordered_json),
resolve_indices() allocated a vector per compared object, and
resolve_members() two. They now use one working vector owned by equal(),
whose capacity is reused, and resolve_indices() needs none when the keys
are unique. resolve_members() sorts small objects by insertion, as the
other paths do.

Instructions per comparison (callgrind, GCC 13 and clang 18, x86-64):
twitter, ordered_json view == ordered_json: 0.939 / 0.941; 20000 small
objects with a duplicate key: 0.741-0.768; all other rows (json,
citm_catalog, canada, view == view) within 0.988-1.003.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

---------

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

message:
* json_view: check_utf8 skips well-formed runs with the parser's string scan

Strings of 32 bytes or more that are written into an editable document
are validated with scan_string_run(), which skips well-formed UTF-8 16
bytes at a time; the byte-wise check runs only from where the scan found
ill-formed UTF-8, to report the same type_error.316. Shorter strings
keep the byte-wise check (inlined with a constant start, so that this
path is the code it was), where the vector scan costs more than it
saves.

set()/push_back() of strings of 32 bytes or more take 0.29-0.76 of the
time (x86-64 GCC, averaged over code layouts) and 0.25-0.80 (AArch64
clang); shorter strings take 1.5-4 % fewer instructions; the json_view
rows of bench_edit execute at most 0.04 % more instructions.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* tests: avoid sign conversion in json_view_edit UTF-8 check

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* json_view: use while in check_utf8_bytewise
