message:
* Document the contract of object keys passed to json_sax::key and key callbacks

Describe what the name passed to json_sax::key and to a parser callback
for parse_event_t::key holds when parsing JSON text: escapes are decoded
to UTF-8, different spellings of a name yield identical strings, the name
is validated before the call (invalid escapes or UTF-8 give a parse error
and no key event), no normalization or case conversion is applied, the
event precedes the ':' check, and duplicate names are reported once per
occurrence. Also note that sax_parse passes binary-format keys unchanged.

See discussion #5955.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Add a test for the object key contract and correct the BON8 note

Pin the guarantees documented for json_sax::key and the key event of
parser callbacks: decoded names, validation before delivery, delivery
before the colon, one event per repeated name, and the binary formats.
BON8 rejects ill-formed UTF-8 in a name even with sax_parse, so the
note no longer lists it with the formats that pass bytes through.

See discussion #5955.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Fix the GCC build of the object key contract test

GCC 11 in C++11 mode rejects a default argument on a lambda parameter
(-Wc++14-extensions) and ignores a static_cast<void> on the
warn_unused_result of parse(). Pass the input format explicitly and bind
the parse result to a variable.

message:
* json_view: source positions in materialize() with JSON_DIAGNOSTIC_POSITIONS

With JSON_DIAGNOSTIC_POSITIONS, materialize() now gives every value the
start_pos()/end_pos() that basic_json::parse() would give it, so exceptions
about materialized values name the same bytes (#5864).

- json_sax_dom_parser takes the lexer type as a defaulted template
  parameter; materialize() passes position_source, which reports the
  positions it derives from the index. diagnostic_positions treats npos as
  "no position" and keeps ranges all-or-nothing.
- Strings with escapes keep the offset of their opening quote plus one in

  string is within the text.

exceptions still carry no byte range, so the tests that compare them with
those of materialized values skip it under the macro, as they skip the path
under JSON_DIAGNOSTICS.

author: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
message:
* Fix self-aliasing in json_pointer::operator/= and patch_inplace

json_pointer::operator/=(const json_pointer&) passed iterators into its
own token vector to insert() when a pointer was appended to itself
(p /= p), which is undefined behavior; libstdc++ produced "/a/b//" for
"/a/b". The pointer now appends a copy in that case.

basic_json::patch_inplace iterated the patch while changing *this, so
j.patch_inplace(j) read freed memory. It now applies a copy of the
patch when the patch is the value itself. A patch stored inside the
value remains undefined behavior and is documented as such; copying the
patch unconditionally would double the time of a large patch.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Fix JSON_DIAGNOSTICS test crash and clang-tidy hit in patch_inplace self-aliasing

The spare-capacity test reallocated non-empty elements through get_ref(), which leaves stale parent pointers under JSON_DIAGNOSTICS; reserve while the array is empty instead. Suppress performance-unnecessary-copy-initialization for the copy that is needed because *this is modified.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Detect a patch stored inside the patched value with JSON_DIAGNOSTICS

patch_inplace applied a copy only when the patch was the value itself. With JSON_DIAGNOSTICS the parent pointers make it cheap to also detect a patch nested inside the value, so that case is handled the same way. Without diagnostics it stays documented undefined behavior.

author: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
message:
* Keep the value unchanged when operator[] with a JSON pointer throws

The non-const operator[](json_pointer) is documented with strong exception
safety, but get_unchecked created intermediate values while walking the
pointer and kept them when a later reference token failed, e.g.
json j; j["/a/99999999999999999999999"_json_pointer] threw 404 and left
{"a":[]}; padding an existing array or appending with "-" behaved alike,
and so did std::length_error/std::bad_alloc from a huge index.

get_unchecked now only walks existing values up to the last reference
token. The last token's key insertion or array growth is strongly
exception safe by itself. Any other change goes through
get_unchecked_create, which records the one change it makes to an existing
value (null converted, key inserted, array grown) in a RAII guard and
reverts it if a later step throws; everything else it creates lies below
that change. The guard needs no try/catch, so JSON_NOEXCEPTION builds are
unaffected. Successful calls create the same values as before.

Docs: state the guarantee in the exceptions list and version history of
operator[], fix the complexity of the pointer overloads of operator[] and
at, and warn that padding arrays up to an untrusted index allocates memory
proportional to the index (operator[].md, untrusted_input.md).

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Make the strongly exception-safe pointer operator[] faster than before

The previous commit made get_unchecked strongly exception safe but slower
with GCC 16 when it creates values (up to +6 % instructions for appending
with "-"). This restructures it so that no benchmark row is slower than
before the strong guarantee, with GCC 16, Clang 22 and Apple Clang.

- get_unchecked walks existing values in one loop that inserts nothing.
  The last reference token is resolved in that walk: "-" appends with
  emplace_back(), an index grows the array with operator[], and a missing
  key is inserted with emplace_hint() at the position the walk's
  lower_bound() found, so the key is searched once.
- With std::less<string_t> or std::less<> as comparator, the walk checks
  the key at the lower bound for equality instead of equivalence, which is
  the same for these comparators and cheaper.
- get_unchecked_create (not inlined) handles all other changes. Its guard
  swaps a null value with a fresh null value instead of copying it and
  reverts the change in a non-inlined function, so a successful call pays
  one compare for it. As every null value converted afterwards is a fresh
  one, it is converted in place instead of assigning a new array or object.
- Keys are added to new objects with emplace(), which also replaces the
  basic_json::operator[] call for ordered_json.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Fix rollback of pointer operator[] for unusual object and string types

Follow-up to the strong exception guarantee of the non-const
operator[](json_pointer):

- get_unchecked_create assumed that emplace() always inserts the key that
  the walk did not find. For object types whose lookup and emplace()
  disagree (e.g. a copied fifo_map), nothing was inserted, the rollback
  erased the existing member, and the walk continued with a value of the
  wrong type (assertion, type_error.305, or a crash). It now checks the
  result of emplace(), arms the rollback only if a key was inserted, and
  otherwise continues the walk with the member found, as basic_json's
  operator[] does: such pointers throw out_of_range.404 and leave the value
  unchanged, as before the strong guarantee.
- The rollback erased the inserted key by key, which converts string_t to
  object_t::key_type and may allocate inside a noexcept function
  (std::terminate on bad_alloc with custom key types). It now erases by the
  iterator emplace() returned, and shrinks a grown array with erase() at
  the end instead of resize(). The documentation states the remaining
  requirement for custom template parameters.
- Creating values no longer calls string_t::begin(), so the non-const
  operator[](json_pointer) compiles with string types that lack it (as the
  alternative string type of the tests).
- Correct the @throw lists of get_unchecked and get_unchecked_create.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Address review comments on operator[](json_pointer) rollback

- undo() shrinks the array with resize() instead of erase()
- comments say what "will be" done in get_unchecked_create
- tests: avoid a clang-tidy performance-unnecessary-copy-initialization
  hit (unit-alt-string) and the word "access" in section names, which
  Flawfinder flags as race/access

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Let the pointer rollback guard call undo() unconditionally

The check in the destructor and JSON_HEDLEY_NEVER_INLINE on undo() made no
measurable difference: instruction counts of j[ptr] are identical with
GCC 13 -O3 and within 0.4 % with clang, timings are within noise.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

message:
* json_view: the library's std conversions read views directly

The library's from_json() overloads (containers, maps, std::array, C
arrays, pairs, tuples, optional, valarray, forward_list, enums, binary,
paths, and scalars) accept views: their traits use the view's
basic_json type, and the few accesses that differ (get_ptr) go through
small helpers. from_json() of a view now finds them; only the probe
still looks up by ADL only. get<T>() of a view thus converts these types
without materialize(), with the same values and exceptions; from an
object, a repeated key keeps the last value, as parse() does.

The view keeps its direct paths for vectors of the types it converts
directly (faster than from_json()) and for containers of views; its
other vector and map paths are replaced by from_json(). For basic_json,
std::valarray and std::forward_list are read in one pass (40 % and 3.5 %
fewer instructions); all other conversions are unchanged.

every comparison. The node and image layouts are unchanged.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* json_view: node_kind in the node writers, spell out read_only, comment fixes

The builder and the edit functions take and store a node_kind instead of
casting a value_t; the numbering assertions and the comments now speak of
node_kind, and the link kind notes that it follows value_t::discarded.
The read-only aliases name view_mode::read_only like the editable ones.
view_mode.md says the mode is a compile-time property of the type.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* json_view: views of read-only documents convert to editable views

A read-only document has no edits, so a view of it reads correctly as a
view of an editable document before its first edit. The implicit
conversion lets a function taking a json_editable_view accept the views
of both modes. There is no conversion the other way: a read-only view of
an editable document would read wrong values after the next edit.

The mode comparisons in the cross-mode operator==/!= use an
is_other_mode trait, which astyle keeps compact.

message:
* Read ND-arrays of half floats and enforce the char limit in ND-arrays

BJData N-dimensional arrays with element type 'h' (float16) failed to
read with a misleading parse_error.112, because the reader's dtype name
table lacked 'h'. It now maps to "half", the JData name. The writer still
does not pack "half"; such an object is written as a plain object and
reads back equal.

BJData limits 'C' (char) to 0..127 in Draft 2 and Draft 3, and the 1-D
reader enforces this, but ND-arrays with _ArrayType_ "char" wrote values
up to 255 as 'C' elements and read them back without a check. The writer

author: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
message:
* Write and read the inner length of BSON binary subtype 0x02

The BSON specification defines the payload of the "binary (old)" subtype
0x02 as an int32 followed by that many bytes. to_bson wrote the plain
payload instead, so decoders such as pymongo and libbson-based readers
rejected the bytes, and from_bson returned the inner length as part of the
payload (documented as lenient behavior in gh-5333).

The writer now emits the outer length (payload + 4), the subtype, the inner
int32 holding the payload size, and the payload. The reader requires an
outer length of at least 4 and an inner length equal to the outer length
minus 4 (the cases the bson-corpus lists as decode errors), reports parse
error 112 otherwise, and returns only the payload. Both directions change
together so that the round trip keeps working.

The single-reservation fast path for scalar entries declines subtype 0x02
because it has no room for the inner length.

This is a deliberate exception to the opt-in rule for behavior changes:
the previous output was invalid BSON.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Check the declared BSON document size before reading its content

The BSON reader compared a document's declared size with the number of bytes
read only when it reached the terminator. The declared size never bounded
the reads, so a SAX handler saw the keys and values of a document whose size
was too small before parse error 112 was reported.

The container frame now stores the position where the document ends
according to its declared size. open_bson_document rejects a size below 5
(size prefix plus terminator) and an embedded document that does not end
before the terminator of its enclosing document; the element loop rejects an
element whose type byte leaves no room for the name terminator and the
document terminator. The terminator check stays and still catches a declared
size that is too large. No input that was accepted before is rejected now;
documents with a wrong size are reported earlier, with fewer SAX events, a
different byte position and, in three cases, a different message. The error
id (parse_error.112) is unchanged and strict=false still does not skip the
check.

The tests that asserted the old messages and positions are updated, with the
outer sizes of two inputs corrected so that they still exercise the embedded
document. New tests cover the SAX events, a size below 5, and an embedded
document that fits exactly.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Document BSON subtype 0x02, document size checks, and lenient reads

Describe the inner length of binary subtype 0x02 that to_bson now writes and
from_bson checks and removes. Add the document size checks (parse_error.112,
not affected by strict=false) to bson.md and from_bson.md, and extend the
list of lenient reads with the UUID and MD5 payload lengths (not checked),
duplicate keys (last value wins), embedded NUL bytes in strings, and the
ignored trailing bytes with strict=false. State that the members of an object
are written in iteration order.

Correct the statement that element names are never validated on read: they
are checked and sanitized like string values by the error handler. Add the
BSON message to the examples of out_of_range.415 and type_error.321, the
subtype limit of 255 to the binary values page, CBOR to the formats that use
byte_container_with_subtype, and fix a typo in the incomplete mapping box.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Regenerate single_include and apply astyle

Result of make amalgamate (including make pretty) for the preceding changes.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Address review of the BSON documentation

Describe exactly when a too small document size is detected and note that subtype 2 data written by earlier versions is not readable.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* docs: use the Oxford comma, drop discarded-value remarks

Add the serial comma in a list added by this PR and remove the BSON
example of type_error.321 (with the type_error.317 remark) so the docs do
not mention discarded values for BSON; restore the original singular
heading of that section. No tables were changed by this PR.

* Fix -Weffc++ in the BSON recorder test and a clang-tidy use-auto hit

author: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
message:
* Validate the optimized-container type marker for count 0 in UBJSON and BJData

The '$' type marker of an optimized container was only checked when an
element was read, so containers with count 0 accepted any marker:
`[$x#i0`, `{$x#i0` and `[$E#i0` parsed as empty containers although a
non-empty container with the same marker is rejected and the UBJSON
specification requires a legal marker after '$'.

get_ubjson_size_type() now checks the marker right after '$' against the
allowed set (UBJSON: Z N T F i U I l L d D H C S [ {; BJData: B U i u I m
l M L h d D C, with the existing exclusion of T F Z N S H [ {) and reports
parse_error.112 "marker ... is not a permitted optimized array type".

Input that was accepted and is now rejected: an optimized container with
count 0 and an invalid '$' type marker. Valid input is unaffected. Two
existing tests that used an invalid marker incidentally ("[$#" and a
negative-count case) were adapted.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Correct and complete the UBJSON documentation

Fix statements that disagree with the behavior (checked with probes):
- `Z` is null; the unused marker is `N`.
- `$` requires `#`; use_type with use_size=false throws other_error.502 only
  for non-empty arrays, objects and binary values.
- NaN and infinity are written as IEEE 754 float64 and read back unchanged;
  the UBJSON specification encodes infinity as null.
- `H` is documented (semantics, parse_error.115, out_of_range.406); the
  "complete mapping" claim is qualified.
- use_type "same type" means same marker.
- Long Z/T/F arrays lose only the `$` annotation; the `#` count and the
  element markers are kept.
- from_ubjson lists the 112, 113, 115, 406 and 408 causes that occur for
  UBJSON, without the BJData-only ND-array wording.
- Duplicate object keys keep the last value; the `$` type marker is
  validated even for count 0.
- Smaller fixes: float32 row, "map" -> "object", https link, exception 110
  strict case, to_ubjson history of discarded values.

author: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
message:
* Skip CBOR tags in front of map keys and validate indefinite text chunks

A tag in front of a text string map key was rejected with parse_error.113
even with cbor_tag_handler_t::ignore or store, although tags in front of
values are handled. The tags are now skipped iteratively before the key is
read; the handler error still rejects them.

The chunks of an indefinite-length text string were concatenated before
the single UTF-8 check, so a code point split over two chunks, or an
invalid chunk, was accepted. RFC 8949, Section 3.2.3 requires every chunk
to be valid on its own. With error_handler_t::strict, replace and ignore
each chunk is now checked; keep is unchanged. The chunks are appended with
append(ptr, len), so StringType needs nothing new.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* docs: correct and extend the CBOR documentation

Fix the negative-integer rows (they used MessagePack boundaries), the
number_integer range of the 0x1B row, and the half-precision entry in the
list of unused types; correct the NaN history (0xF9 since 3.8.0) and the
tagged-item wording (only the tag directly in front of a byte string is
stored, and only in the 0xD8..0xDB form). Document that to_cbor is not
RFC 8949 deterministic, that duplicate keys are accepted (last wins),
tags in front of keys, per-chunk UTF-8 validation, the exceptions
parse_error.113, out_of_range.406/408 of from_cbor, the pointer and
C array input traps, the partially written output on exceptions, and the
store/ignore results in the binary values example. Drop the claim that
the CBOR reader needs StringType::append(const StringType&) and
BinaryType::insert(pos, first, last).

author: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
message:
* create objects for tokens that cannot be array indices (#5357)

When operator[](json_pointer) traverses a level that does not exist yet,
the null value is turned into an array or an object depending on the
reference token. The check only tested whether all characters are digits,
so tokens that can never be a valid array index selected an array and
then failed:

- "01" (and any other token with a leading '0') threw parse_error.106
- the empty token threw out_of_range.404

Both tokens are valid object keys, and both work when the level already
exists as an object, so creating the level changed the outcome. Test the
token against the RFC 6901, Sect. 4 grammar for array indices instead, so
that such tokens create an object. This only affects pointers that threw
before.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Clarify that the token 0 is a valid array index in operator[] docs

The note described valid array indices as "a nonempty sequence of digits
without a leading 0", which read literally excludes the token "0" itself,
contradicting both the code and the /foo/0/0/0 example in the next
sentence. Spell out the RFC 6901 grammar instead.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* docs: cross-reference json_view and json_document for 3.13.0

Document the new zero-copy document/view API across the docs: add a
"Documents and views" section to the basic_json API hub linking to all
specializations, point parsing/conversion/modifying pages to the view-based
alternatives, add document/view sections to feature pages, update the
landing page to mention json_view.hpp/json_literals.hpp, and cross-link
debugging/exceptions.

Also document wide-string inputs (and ill-formed UTF-16/32 rejection),
add parse/accept examples for wide strings, fix related doc gaps, and
align features/parsing and FAQ with the added support.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* docs: fix article before std::istream in FAQ

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* docs: clarify document inputs, decoding, get<T>() and editing

Address review comments: say which inputs are borrowed and that a wide
string pointer is an extra input, which values are decoded during parsing,
that get<T>() reads only built-in types directly, all forms of set() and
that the document's insert() is array-only, and how to store wide strings.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* docs: integers are converted while parsing a document

Also say "They accept every input" in basic_json_document::parse.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

message:
* from_json: number-first dispatch for arithmetic types, loop for std::array (#5891)

from_json(ArithmeticType&) now reads numbers through get_number_value() and
handles a boolean on a cold path, which puts the three number types first in
the per-element type dispatch.

get<std::array<T, N>>() always took the identity_tag overload, a pack
expansion of N calls j.at(i).get<T>() that clang unrolls into straight-line
code (about 28,000 instructions for N = 1000), so its speed depended on
inlining decisions in that body. For trivial element types, which cannot tell
default construction plus assignment from construction in place, it now fills
a std::array in a loop. That loop, shared with get_to(), checks the size once
and reads the inner array directly; a short array still converts the elements
it has and then throws the out_of_range error at() would throw.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Skip the get_to result check without exceptions

Without exceptions, the get_to calls in CHECK_THROWS_WITH_AS do not run,
so the array keeps its initial values (ci_test_noexceptions).

message:
* Reserve the parser's nesting stack once

The stack of open arrays and objects was a std::vector<std::uint8_t> that
allocated at the first push_back and then reallocated at 1, 2, 4, 8 bytes,
so a document nested four levels deep made four allocations before it
parsed a value. A document that starts with a container now reserves 32
levels in one allocation; deeper documents grow as before. The loop that
reads the tokens is the code it was, so large documents are not affected
(a stack object with its own storage, and a reserve at every container,
both cost the token loop instructions or cycles).

Fixed cost of parsing a 124-byte object (macOS instructions): accept
-7.6 %, DOM -2.5 %; no change for a single number.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Build arrays of the DOM parser in one exact-size allocation

Reading an array of unknown length appended its elements to a std::vector
one at a time, so a small array reallocated (and moved its elements) at
sizes 1, 2, 4, ... The DOM SAX parser now collects the elements of arrays
whose length is unknown on one stack shared by all open arrays and moves
them into an array of exactly the right size when the closing bracket
arrives. An array that grows past 16 elements switches to appending to its
own vector, so large arrays pay no second copy. Binary formats, which
announce the length, and builds with JSON_DIAGNOSTICS or
JSON_DIAGNOSTIC_POSITIONS (whose values need their final place from the
start) keep storing into the array directly.

The stacks of open containers are reserved on first use instead of growing
from one element.

The binary readers get a DOM parser of their own, json_sax_dom_binary_parser:
it is the plain parser that stores every value directly in its container
(the code the readers used before). Their containers announce their size, so
the bookkeeping of the collecting parser (frame entries, the destination of a
finished container) was pure overhead for them: with the collecting parser
FromBinaryShape nested was 3-12 % and containers up to 5 % more instructions
(GCC) than before. With the plain parser Linux Ir of FromBinaryShape and
FromBinaryBuffer is within 0.8 % of develop (Clang: identical).

canada.json has 56 000 two-element arrays that took three allocations each
and now take two. DOM parse Ir on Linux against develop (GCC / Clang): canada
-7.0 % / -7.7 %, citm -0.8 % / -1.6 %, 124-byte object -5.4 % / -5.5 %;
accept and SAX are untouched.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Reuse one value for the key events of the callback parser

parse() with a callback built a new string value for every key it passed to
the callback (a heap allocation and release per key), and copied the key a
second time into the object. The callback parser now keeps one string value
for key events, which it assigns, and moves the key into the object.

Callback parse, Linux Ir (GCC / Clang): twitter -13.3 % / -11.7 %, citm
-9.5 % / -7.6 %. (Earlier macOS measurement: twitter -19.5 % instructions.)

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Remember where the DOM parser stores the next value

The DOM SAX parser looked up the innermost open container for every value:
the end of its frame stack, then the object or array pointer in the frame.
Compilers have to reload all of that after each value is stored, since a
store of a value may alias the frame. The parser now keeps the innermost
container's kind and, for an array that stores directly, the array itself
in members, updated when a container opens or closes.

Flat arrays of numbers are the case that mattered: parsing floats.json
(1 000 000 doubles) into a DOM took 2 % more cycles than before the
previous commit on macOS and now takes 0.4 % fewer than the code before it
(signed_ints.json -0.8 %). Linux Ir is unchanged (canada -6.1 % GCC /
-6.9 % Clang, citm -0.3 % / -0.8 %, twitter +0.2 % / 0.0 %).

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Look up the keys of big ordered_json objects in a hash table

ordered_map keeps its elements in a vector and searches it linearly for
every key it adds, so parsing an object with n keys into ordered_json took
O(n^2) key comparisons: 33 billion instructions for one object with 30 000
keys, where json needs 245 million. From 64 keys on, the DOM parser now
keeps a hash table of the keys of the open object (hashes and positions
only; the elements stay in the vector) and finds duplicate keys there. The
result is the same, including the position of a key that occurs twice.
Smaller objects, std::map based objects and key types without std::hash
are untouched.

ordered_json parse, macOS instructions: object with 1 000 keys 64.8 M ->
14.6 M, 10 000 keys 5 104 M -> 38.7 M, 30 000 keys 33 358 M -> 89 M.
Linux Ir of an object with 2 000 keys: 43.0 M -> 1.9 M (GCC), 37.9 M ->
1.8 M (Clang).

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Trim the work the DOM parser does per container and per member

Opening and closing an array or object cost the DOM parser more than before
the exact-size array change, which showed on documents of many small
objects (jeopardy.json: +1.4 % Ir with GCC). This takes it back:

- the stack of open containers keeps its first eight entries in the parser
  object instead of in a vector, so it needs no capacity check beyond the
  push itself and no allocation for typical documents;
- a container is created in the place it ends up in, instead of as a
  temporary that is then moved there;
- a new object member, which is null, is constructed over the null instead
  of being swapped with it (only with the default base class of basic_json);
- the key index that big ordered_json objects use is only a part of the
  stack entries of objects that can have one;
- an array that outgrows the stack reserves twice what it has so far, as a
  vector that grew by itself would have.

DOM parse Ir of the series up to here against develop, Linux GCC / Clang:
canada -6.6 % / -7.3 %, citm +1.2 % / +0.2 %, jeopardy +0.4 % / -0.1 %,
124-byte object -6.5 % / -6.2 %. (twitter measures +6.8 % / +6.6 % at this
point in steady state, almost all of it in glibc's malloc/consolidate for the
new allocation sizes; with the last commit of the series it is -0.1 % / 0.0 %.)

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Test parsing containers of the sizes where the DOM parser changes storage

The DOM parser collects the elements of an array on a stack (up to 16) and
the members of an ordered_json object (up to 32) before it moves them into
the container, and uses a hash table for keys from 64 members on. Parse
arrays and objects of the sizes around these limits, nested into each other,
with repeated keys, and as random trees that are built next to their text,
and compare json and ordered_json against the value built through the API.

The tests pass on the code from before these changes as well. The random
trees are what finds the mistakes that are easy to make here: while the
collecting change was being written, a collected array that outgrew the
stack at the moment its parent had just reached the limit left its elements
in the parent, and only these tests (142 failed assertions) showed it.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Do not convert floats that cannot overflow in accept()

accept() only has to find out whether a float token is finite: json_sax_acceptor
ignores the value, and the parser rejects only a float that overflows. A
float whose digits fit into 19 digits and whose decimal exponent is at most
max_exponent10 - 19 is below 10^max_exponent10 and cannot overflow, so the
lexer, told by accept() that the value is not needed, skips the conversion
for those. A token that may overflow, with more digits, or in another float
format is converted as before, so 1e309 and its neighbours are rejected as
they were (the new test compares accept() with parse() on tokens around the
limit).

json::accept(): canada.json Ir -8.6 % (GCC) / -10.9 % (Clang), 124-byte
object -3.2 %; cycles on the M1 (release benchmarks, LTO): canada -7.8 %,
floats.json -9.0 %. The check tests the accept() flag first, so the parser
that needs the value pays one load and branch: SaxParse canada +0.35 % Ir
(GCC and Clang), DOM canada +0.4 %.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Collect the members of ordered_json objects on a stack until they are known

An ordered_json object keeps its members in a vector and appends every new
member to it, so reading an object of unknown size reallocated the vector at
1, 2, 4, 8, ... members, and ordered_map copies all keys on every
reallocation. The DOM SAX parser now collects the members of such objects on
one stack shared by all open objects, as it does the elements of arrays, and
moves them into a vector of exactly the right size when the closing brace
arrives. An object that gets past 32 members switches to appending to its
own vector (and, from 64, to the key index of the earlier commit). The
members are the same, in the same order, and a key that occurs twice keeps
the place of its first occurrence. std::map based objects, objects whose
size the input announces (binary formats), and builds with JSON_DIAGNOSTICS
or JSON_DIAGNOSTIC_POSITIONS are untouched.

What only ordered objects need (the collected members, the key indexes) is
a member of the parser only for them, and the code that stores a value tries
the array that takes its elements directly first. An array that outgrows
the stack now reserves 32 elements, the capacity a vector that grew by
itself has at that point; with the larger reserve before, parsing
floats.json (1 000 000 numbers) was 2 % slower on Apple M1 than before this
series.

ordered_json parse, Linux Ir against develop (GCC / Clang): citm -11.6 % /
-11.7 %, twitter -8.4 % / -8.4 %, jeopardy (12 000 objects of 7 keys)
-10.5 % / -8.0 %, canada -3.9 % / -5.2 %, 124-byte object -20.9 % / -16.5 %.
macOS time (M1, earlier base): citm -19 %, twitter -13 %, jeopardy -13 %,
canada -14 %, 124-byte object -26 %. json parse: steady-state twitter -0.1 %
(see the previous commits), citm -1.2 %.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Rename the key index's match callback so Flawfinder doesn't read it as std::equal

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Bind the parser test's strings by reference in the range-for loop

GCC and Clang 14 (-Wrange-loop-construct) reported the copy.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Collect container values only in basic_json's own parse functions

A json_sax_dom_parser that a user constructs (as in the sax_no_exception
example) must hold the values read before a parse error, as on develop:
its value is used after the error. The values of containers of unknown
size are now collected on a stack only with the new template parameter
Collect (default false), which json::parse() and the json_view
materialization set; without it, every value is stored in place as it
arrives. A test checks the values kept after an error for json and
ordered_json.

Also fixes the clang-tidy, cpplint and Infer findings: the frame stack
keeps its first frames in a std::array (left uninitialized) and the
others in a std::unique_ptr, auto for create<>(), NOLINT for member
initializers -Weffc++ needs, and an @infer-ignore for the nullptr that
place_container() does not use.

json::parse() and ordered_json::parse() instructions are unchanged
(Apple clang; twitter, citm, canada, jeopardy: -0.03 % to +0.25 %).

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Clarify the DOM parser's collection stacks and rename reenter_enclosing_container()

Address review comments: explain why a closed container erases only the top
of the shared stack, set the payload before the type, rename the helper that
makes the enclosing container current again, and declare the parser's state
stack right before reserving it.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Export json_sax_dom_parser from the C++20 module for MSVC

MSVC needs the detail classes that basic_json befriends to be visible in
the module (#3970, as json_sax_dom_callback_parser); with its new
template parameter, json_sax_dom_parser failed in ci_module_cpp20
(C2039, not a member of nlohmann::detail).

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Keep the overflow-limit numbers of the parser test in a std::vector

clang-tidy (cppcoreguidelines-avoid-c-arrays) rejected the C array.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Fix the clang-tidy findings of the ordered_json parser tests

The container sizes are a std::array, the expected text uses raw string
literals, the generator's arithmetic is in parentheses, auto for the
result of make<>(), and single characters are appended as characters.
clang-tidy now reports nothing on the lines the branch adds to
unit-ordered_json.cpp and unit-class_parser.cpp (apart from checks CI's
clang-tidy does not have).

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

message:
* Read C streams into a json_document in blocks

json_document::parse(FILE*) (and read(), accept(), parse_copy()) went through the
library's file input adapter and appended the text character by character
with fgetc. Read it with fread in blocks instead, like the std::istream
overload already does.

Parsing citm_catalog.json (1.7 MB) from a FILE*:
  Apple M1: 80.6 M -> 8.4 M instructions, 4.8 ms -> 0.55 ms (parse of the same text from a std::string: 8.7 M)
  Linux x86-64 Ir (whole run), GCC 13 / Clang 18: 47.0 M -> 13.7 M / 45.8 M -> 14.2 M
The parsed documents and the error cases are identical (checked over the test corpus
and 30 mutants of each file). A null FILE* is handled as before (by the library's adapter).

Belongs to the PR "json_view: read-side speedups".

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Index arrays without subtrees directly

operator[](idx), at(idx) and back() skipped the elements of an array one
after the other, whatever they were. In an array none of whose elements is
an array or object (numbers, strings, booleans, null) the elements are
adjacent nodes, which the array node's own sizes tell: its subtree has
exactly one node more than it has elements. Such an element is now the
node idx after the array node; any other array is walked as before.

Reading r[i] for every i of an array of 3000 integers:
  Apple M1: 28.8 M instructions, 3.1 ms -> 0.1 M instructions, 4 us
  Linux x86-64 Ir (whole run), GCC 13 / Clang 18: 84.1 M -> 3.1 M / 75.0 M -> 3.0 M
Arrays that contain arrays are unchanged.

Belongs to the PR "json_view: read-side speedups".

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Skip the bounds checks of number and string tokens in NUL-terminated input

For a NUL-terminated input (std::string, C string, string literal), the
parser reads the terminator instead of comparing p with the end, via
cursor::cur(). Number and string scanning still tested `p != e` before each
look at the next byte (after the integer digits for '.', for 'e', after
the exponent sign and digits, and after a string for its closing quote),
although the terminator can never be one of those characters. They now use
cur(), which is the plain load for NUL-terminated input and the bounds check
for ptr+len input, as before.

Parsing, Apple M1 instructions per parse: twitter 3.126 M -> 3.089 M (-1.2 %),
citm_catalog 8.70 M -> 8.58 M (-1.3 %), jeopardy 306.1 M -> 302.5 M (-1.2 %), signed
integers 281 M -> 266 M (-5.4 %), canada and floats -0.1 % / -0.9 %.
Linux x86-64 Ir, GCC 13 / Clang 18: twitter -0.5 % / -0.0 %, signed integers +0.2 % / -0.7 %.

Belongs to the PR "json_view: read-side speedups".

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Make the index text of items() on arrays lazy

basic_json_view::items() on an array formatted every element's index with
std::to_string when the item was made, whether or not the loop asks for the
key. The item now keeps the position and makes the text on the first key()
call. Objects are not affected.

Iterating over the items of an array of 3000 numbers and reading only the values:
  Apple M1: 25.5 us -> 4.6 us (0.45 M -> ~0 net instructions)
  Linux x86-64 Ir (whole run), GCC 13 / Clang 18: 14.9 M -> 4.1 M / 15.3 M -> 4.6 M
Reading key() costs what it did (24.5 us).

Belongs to the PR "json_view: read-side speedups".

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Make the default of value() with a C string only if the member is missing

basic_json_view::value(key, "text") and value(pointer, "text") built a
std::string from the default first and passed it on, so a call allocated
for the default even when the member exists, and copied it again when it
does not. They now look the member up and make the result directly: from the
member if there is one, else from the C string. Behavior, including the
exceptions, is the same.

Two calls (member found, member missing) with a 40 character default, Apple M1:
  1.6 K -> 0.7 K instructions
  Linux x86-64 Ir (500 rounds), GCC 13 / Clang 18: 2.46 M -> 2.22 M / 2.40 M -> 2.15 M

Belongs to the PR "json_view: read-side speedups".

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Materialize scalars directly and keep the stack of small subtrees local

basic_json_view::materialize() (and get<BasicJsonType>()) always set up the
SAX handler that parse() uses and a std::vector for the open containers,
sized from the document's deepest nesting. For a scalar, which is most of what
is materialized one value at a time, neither is needed: the value is made
directly (the same constructors the handler ends up calling). For arrays and
objects the stack of open containers is now a local array for the first 16
levels, and the vector is only used for deeper documents.

Materializing five scalars of a small document, Apple M1: 3.6 K -> 0.9 K instructions
  Linux x86-64 Ir (500 rounds), GCC 13 / Clang 18: 2.96 M -> 2.37 M / 2.90 M -> 2.29 M

Belongs to the PR "json_view: read-side speedups".

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Copy the text between escapes while scanning it

A string that contains an escape is decoded by builder::slow_string(). After
each escape it scanned the next run of plain bytes (8 or 16 byte-by-byte
steps, then a vector loop), and then copied that run to the decode arena in a
second pass. The run is now copied 16 bytes at a time while it is scanned
(one vector load, a store of the same 16 bytes, and the mask of the bytes
that end the run), and the write position lives in a local variable, not in
the builder, since a store of a character may alias the builder's members and
made the compiler reload it after every escape. A run that ends at a quote
needs no scan, and non-ASCII text goes through the UTF-8 check as before;
the portable code is unchanged.

Parsing, Apple M1 instructions: jeopardy.json 304.0 M -> 293.8 M (-3.4 %), 3000 strings with
escapes 1.72 M -> 1.54 M (-10 %), twitter -0.6 %.
Linux x86-64 Ir, GCC 13 / Clang 18: escaped strings -7.6 % / -11.4 %, twitter 0.0 % / 0.0 %.
Documents and error messages are identical on 900 k random strings of escapes, UTF-8 and control
characters (also under ASan), and on mutants of the test corpus.

Belongs to the PR "json_view: read-side speedups".

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Hash the last bytes of a key of a large object without a loop

key_hash() mixed a key eight bytes at a time and then packed the remaining
0-7 bytes one by one, in a loop. The last word of a key of eight or more
bytes is now read as the last eight bytes of the key (overlapping the word
before), and a key of 2-7 bytes as two overlapping words of four or two
bytes. A product only moves bits upwards, and the slot is taken from the low
bits: the high bits of the last word are folded down before the
multiplication, since keys that differ only in their last characters ("user_17",
"user_18") would otherwise share slots. The hash is not stored, so its values
may change.

Looking up every key of an object of 1000 random keys, Apple M1 instructions per 1000 lookups:
  keys of 5 bytes 175 K -> 93 K, hex strings of 8 bytes 177 K -> 168 K, keys of 12 bytes 196 K -> 186 K
Linux x86-64 Ir (whole run), GCC 13 / Clang 18: 5-byte keys -4.7 % / -8.8 %, 12-byte keys -3.3 % / -7.4 %.
Building the tables while parsing such objects is cheaper as well (5-byte keys: 13.3 us -> 10.1 us).

Belongs to the PR "json_view: read-side speedups".

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Compare short keys of a large object without a call of memcmp

find_indexed() compared the key of a member the table points to with
memcmp, a library call for any length. Up to 16 bytes, the bytes are now
compared as two overlapping words (the first and the last 8, 4, or 2 bytes),
as find_member() already does for the objects without a table; longer keys
still use memcmp.

Looking up every key of an object of 1000 random keys, Apple M1 instructions per 1000 lookups
(with the previous commit): keys of 5 bytes 93 K -> 72 K, hex strings of 8 bytes 168 K -> 148 K,
keys of 12 bytes 186 K -> 170 K, keys of 24 bytes 198 K -> 193 K (unchanged, memcmp).
Linux x86-64 Ir (whole run), GCC 13 / Clang 18: 5-byte keys -7.2 % / -7.3 %, 12-byte keys -5.9 % / -6.6 %.

Belongs to the PR "json_view: read-side speedups".

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Read an unedited editable document like a read-only one

Views of a json_editable_document followed edits at every step: the
lookup, the element access, back(), dump() and materialize() were built
for nodes that can be moved or linked, though no edit changes the index until
the first one (every edit creates the edit state before it touches a node).
Until then these now take the read-only code: one check of the document's
edit state per call, not per member or per node. After the first edit
nothing changes. Views that were made earlier keep working, as the check is
made when they are used.

Unedited editable document, Apple M1: dump() of twitter.json 1.40 M -> 1.22 M instructions (-12.6 %);
lookups unchanged. Linux x86-64 Ir, GCC 13 / Clang 18: dump -1.7 % / -1.0 %, lookups -0.1 % / 0.0 %.
Walking with iterators is unchanged, and so is dump() after an edit.

Belongs to the PR "json_view: read-side speedups".

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Format the numbered test keys of json_view's index with a stream

The keys were made with snprintf() and a format from a list, which
Flawfinder reports as an error (CWE-134, a format string that is not a
literal). A stream now formats them; the 30000 keys of the test are the
same as before.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Put the key number of the json_view index test in parentheses

astyle formatted i * step after << as a pointer declaration (i* step),
which failed the amalgamation check.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Fix the compiler and lint findings of json_view's read side and tests

- find() and contains() dispatch on Editable for the member lookup; for
  documents that cannot be edited both branches were the same call
  (GCC -Wduplicated-branches)
- json_view.hpp includes <cstdio> for the FILE overload (cpplint)
- the arena check macro of the builder is on one line (cpplint read it
  as an if body without braces)
- tests: no nested conditional (also MSVC C4018), no useless cast,
  parentheses around mixed operators, raw string literals, += instead
  of temporary concatenations, and NOLINT for the fixed seeds and a
  find() != npos, as elsewhere in the tests

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Grow the decode arena through a function and store its position back on every return

slow_string() kept its write position in locals and grew the arena through
the macro NLOHMANN_VIEW_ENSURE. The macro is now the always-inline member
arena_ensure() (a lambda is not inlined at every call site by clang, which
then keeps the position in memory: +11 % instructions on escape-heavy
strings), and a guard stores the position back into m_arena_write on every
return instead of by hand on the successful one. Instruction counts are
unchanged (clang) or 1 % lower (GCC).

Also word the complexity of back() as that of at().

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

message:
* Write the indented output of json_view's dump() with the fast writer

The compact writer of dump() (cursor in a register, fixed-size copies of
tokens) served dump(-1) only; every dump(indent), and everything with
ensure_ascii that was indented, went through a generic walk that calls put()
for each token and put_repeated() (a memset call) for each line break. The
fast writer now writes indented output, too, with or without ensure_ascii, and
the generic walk is gone. A line break is a copy of a 64-byte ruler (a line
break and 63 indentation characters) when the line is at most 64 bytes, and a
store plus memset beyond that. The depth is counted only in the indented
instantiations (counting it in the compact one cost an editable document 5 %
with Clang). The indented walks are out of line (dump_pretty()): inlined
into dump() next to the compact ones, they made compact dumps of integer
arrays 7 % slower.

A decoded string (one with escape sequences) of a damaged image loaded with
image_check::bounds can contain invalid UTF-8. As before, the compact dump
writes such bytes unchanged, and the indented dump throws type_error.316; its
runs are found by the lexer's validating scan (a scalar validation of every
sequence made dump(2) of decoded CJK text twice as slow as before).

dump(2) instructions per call, macOS arm64 (before -> after):

               twitter         citm            canada          jeopardy(4k)
  json         3.75M -> 1.85M  8.28M -> 3.93M  67.1M -> 56.0M  9.56M -> 4.81M
  editable     3.82M -> 1.84M  8.48M -> 4.02M  68.1M -> 56.2M  9.66M -> 4.75M

Linux instructions (GCC 13 / Clang 18), dump(2) and dump(2, ' ', true):

  twitter      -25 % / -30 %      -11 % / -11 %
  citm         -29 % / -28 %      -24 % / -24 %
  jeopardy(4k) -25 % / -32 %      -20 % / -24 %
  CJK text with \u escapes  -6 % / -11 %   -2 % / -2 %

The compact dump is unchanged (within +0.4 % on Linux, within noise on the Mac).

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Scan the strings of json_view's dump() with ensure_ascii 16 bytes at a time

With ensure_ascii, a string of the source that has a byte >= 0x7F was written
by a generic path: put() per piece and a validate-and-decode step for every
character beyond ASCII. It now goes through a writer with the cursor in a
local variable. The part of the string that has nothing to escape is found
16 bytes at a time (SSE2 or NEON; the existing 8-byte scan without vector
support) and copied; strings that are ASCII throughout are still decided by
the 8-byte check of dump() with ensure_ascii (a 16-byte scan for them was
2-5 % slower for short strings). The two-byte sequences (lead C2..DF) and
the three-byte sequences whose continuation bytes may have any value (lead
E1..EF except ED) are decoded with a few compares; E0, ED, four-byte
sequences, and damaged input go through validate_one_utf8() as before, so
damaged images still throw type_error.316.

dump(-1, ' ', true) instructions per call, macOS arm64 (develop -> now);
the compact dump without ensure_ascii and dumps of ASCII text are unchanged:

  twitter 5.42M -> 3.57M    citm 3.28M -> 3.24M     jeopardy(4k) 5.78M -> 5.65M
  CJK text, raw 66.5M -> 35.3M    escaped \u 32.7M -> 17.0M
  Latin text with accents 11.5M -> 9.4M    ASCII text 4.40M -> 4.40M

Linux instructions (GCC 13 / Clang 18), dump(-1, ' ', true):

  twitter -9 % / -33 %    CJK text -14 % / -47 %    Latin text -8 % / -18 %
  citm -0.2 % / -0.4 %    ASCII text -0.1 % / -0.3 %

The compact dump without ensure_ascii is unchanged (canada 0.0 %).

The unit test covers every character of the Basic Multilingual Plane, and a
character that needs an escape at each position of strings of 0..40 bytes.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Find the end of the plain run of a decoded string 16 bytes at a time with SSE2

The strings of a document that had escape sequences are written in runs
without a quote, backslash, or control character; the compact dump found the
end of a run 8 bytes at a time with a SWAR test. With SSE2 (x86-64) it now
compares 16 bytes per step. NEON keeps the SWAR code: there the mask of a
step costs more than it saves on the short runs that are typical here.

Instructions of dump(), Linux (GCC 13 / Clang 18):

  twitter.json                  1.99M -> 1.88M (-5.2 %) / 1.97M -> 1.92M (-3.0 %)
  CJK text with \u escapes      5.98M -> 4.52M (-24.5 %) / 5.30M -> 4.25M (-19.9 %)
  ASCII text with a few escapes 4.28M -> 4.09M (-4.4 %) / 4.24M -> 4.11M (-3.2 %)
  jeopardy (4,000 questions)    5.08M -> 4.78M (-5.8 %) / 4.97M -> 4.80M (-3.4 %)

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Rename depth_counter's open() and close() to enter() and leave()

Flawfinder took them for the file functions open() and close().

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Fix the clang-tidy findings in json_view's dump and its tests

- the SSE2 loop of the string scan is within NOLINTBEGIN/END
  (portability-simd-intrinsics), as in to_chars.hpp
- depth_counter<false>'s leave() and get() keep the interface of
  depth_counter<true> instead of being static
- write_ascii() compares the room left as a size_t variable
- the test's texts are a std::array, and a JSON fragment with escapes
  is a raw string literal

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Move dump_ascii() and dump_pretty() next to dump()

Address a review comment: the two dispatchers that dump() calls now follow
it directly.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

author: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
message:
* Compare json_view with yyjson, simdjson, and Boost.JSON

tests/benchmarks/json_view/ holds a comparison with other
libraries, answering the question users ask when they pick one.
It is not built by CMake and not run by CI.

- bench_view.cpp: parse, traverse, select and dump of twitter,
  citm_catalog, canada, jeopardy, a tweet and an RPC request,
  against json_view, yyjson, simdjson, Boost.JSON and json::parse,
  all agreeing and run interleaved.
- bench_corpus.cpp: parse, traverse and dump of any file list.
- bench_edit.cpp: parses, edits through each library's own API,
  and serializes; all outputs must describe the same value.
- compare.py: builds both programs with system or pinned,
  SHA-256-checked downloads, and writes results with the commit,
  CPU, OS, compiler and library versions.
- README.md and a workflow that runs on demand or via a PR label.

Fairness fixes folded in: each engine runs once untimed before
each timed round, so the next one no longer pays for the
previous one's cleanup; dump is also compared with source numbers
against yyjson's raw-number mode; a "simdjson DOM (fresh)" column
and a reused-document column for json_view were added;
compare.py's paths are absolute; downloads use a .part file and a
failed checksum removes the archive.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Make the downloads of json_view's compare.py robust

Hash the archives in chunks instead of reading them into memory, download
with a timeout, extract into a temporary directory that is renamed into
place only after success (a half-extracted directory was trusted forever),
and split CXX and CC into arguments so that values like 'ccache g++' work.
Note at the pins that a SHA-256 mismatch of a GitHub tag archive means
that GitHub regenerated it.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Add a timeout and a concurrency group to the json_view benchmarks

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Check the CSV file and the round count in the json_view benchmarks

fopen() of the CSV output was not checked, so an unwritable directory made
fprintf() write to a null FILE*; the round count is parsed with strtol and
clamped instead of atoi.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

author: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
message:
* Flatten into a std::map by inserting next to the previous entry

flatten() added every path with operator[], so each insertion into the
std::map of the result searched the tree from the root and compared long
shared path prefixes, which took half the time on canada.json. Paths come
out in nearly sorted order, so they are now inserted with emplace_hint
next to the entry added last, for object types that have it. ordered_map
keeps its append without lookup, and other object types keep
operator[].

Path segments are also appended in place, without a temporary string
for each escaped key or array index.

flatten() of canada.json, citm_catalog.json and twitter.json is 1.4x to
1.9x as fast; ordered_json is unchanged (1.05x). The output is
unchanged.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Unflatten without splitting keys or walking each path from the root

unflatten() split every key into a vector of reference tokens, stored the
pointer prefixes in a tree to decide which values become arrays, and then
looked up every token of every key from the root again.

Keys are now checked by a scan that raises the same parse_error.107/108 as
split(), skipping the part a key shares with the previous one, which was
checked already. The prefixes that denote arrays are kept in a small hash
set of key slices; the array/object decision is unchanged. The walk keeps
the values along the previous key's path, so only the part of a key that
differs from the previous one is looked up. Keys of a flattened object are
usually sorted, so that part is short.

unflatten() of canada.json, citm_catalog.json and twitter.json is 1.9x to
2.3x as fast; the output and the exceptions are unchanged.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Apply plain JSON Patch operations without building a json_pointer

patch() built a json_pointer for every operation, which splits the path
into a vector of strings, and for "add" and "remove" a second one for
the parent. That took 20% to 45% of the time not spent copying the
document.

"add", "remove", "replace" and "test" with a path that has no escapes and
denotes existing values (the parent, for "add"), as diff() creates them,
are now applied by resolving the path in place, reusing one string for
the reference tokens. Every other operation, and every operation that
would fail, takes the existing code, so the results, the exceptions and
the state left after a failing operation are unchanged.

patch() of the diffs of canada.json, citm_catalog.json and twitter.json
is 1.02x to 1.10x as fast; the rest is the copy of the document.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Build diff operations member by member

diff() created every operation from an initializer list, so each
{"op", "replace"} pair became a temporary array with two heap strings
before it was turned into an object member; an operation took about 25
allocations. The operations are now built as objects whose members are
assigned one by one. Paths of members and elements are also built in
place, without a temporary string for each escaped key or array index.

diff() of canada.json, citm_catalog.json and twitter.json, with every
eighth scalar changed, is 1.3x to 1.6x as fast; the output is unchanged.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Diff objects with the same keys in lockstep and keep one path buffer

diff() looked up every key of the source object in the target object,
and built a new string for the path of every value it descended into.
Objects of the same size usually have the same keys in the same order,
so they are now walked together as long as that holds, without a
lookup; objects that differ fall back to the lookup from the first key
that does not match. The path is one buffer that is extended before
descending and shortened again afterwards. Objects whose members are
equal but in a different order (possible with ordered_json) still get
no operations.

Together with the previous commit, diff() of canada.json,
citm_catalog.json and twitter.json is 1.5x to 2.0x as fast; ordered_json
1.65x to 1.85x. The output is unchanged.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Use std::array for the index buffer in append_index()

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Declare the partner iterator in the loop initializer in diff_object_keys()

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Fix GCC and clang-tidy warnings in the JSON pointer speedups

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

message:
* Use standard library helpers where available, with C++11 fallbacks

Add detail helpers that call the standard library function when the
library provides it (checked with the __cpp_lib_* feature-test macros, so
no new ABI-tag macros) and a C++11 implementation otherwise:

- detail::clamp (std::clamp): by value, so that static constexpr members
  need no out-of-line definition before C++17; used in json_view's dump()
  buffer sizing, where step() can now be a static constexpr member.
- detail::bit_cast (std::bit_cast): replaces dtoa_impl::reinterpret_bits
  and the memcpy bit copies in the number parser, to_chars, the json_view
  serializer, and binary_writer::to_char_type.
- detail::byteswap (std::byteswap): one implementation instead of the
  binary writer's own byte_swap() overloads and the bswap chain in
  to_chars' store_msb_first().
- count_leading_zeros/count_trailing_zeros: two 32-bit _BitScanReverse/
  _BitScanForward calls for MSVC x86/ARM32 instead of the loop, and
  std::countl_zero/countr_zero for compilers without builtins.
- conjunction, disjunction, negation, bool_constant, and uncvref_t map to
  their std counterparts in C++17/C++20.

Builtins and intrinsics stay ahead of the <bit> functions, as MSVC's
std::countl_zero checks for LZCNT at run time unless AVX2 is enabled.

The generated code is unchanged with Clang (C++11/20/23, arm64 and
x86-64) and GCC 16 for parsing, dumping, and the binary formats. The
binary reader keeps its own byte_swap() and the writer its memcpy calls:
the smaller code from detail::byteswap/std::bit_cast there made GCC 16
inline get_number()/write_number() differently, which slowed reading by
10-18 % and writing by about 1 %.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Name the target byte order once (JSON_LITTLE_ENDIAN_TARGET, JSON_BIG_ENDIAN_TARGET)

to_chars.hpp and bit_ops.hpp repeated the long __BYTE_ORDER__/_MSC_VER
conditions; macro_scope.hpp now defines them once (undefined again in
macro_unscope.hpp).

hunk_contexts: inline std::size_t plain_output_run(const unsigned char* s, std::size_t n) noexc
message:
With ensure_ascii, the view's dump wrote every string through the escaping
path, which decodes UTF-8 byte by byte, even strings of the source that are
plain ASCII. A string of the source without escape sequences has no quote,
backslash, or control character, so ensure_ascii leaves it unchanged
exactly when it has no byte >= 0x7F. The dump now checks that eight bytes
at a time (one add and one or per word) and copies such strings like the
dump without ensure_ascii.

The compact walk (dump_compact) now also serves ensure_ascii, through a
separate out-of-line instantiation, so the walk without ensure_ascii keeps
its speed.

Parsing is unchanged. A flag set by the parser would let the dump skip the
check and was about twice as fast for compact output, but it costs every
parse of string-heavy input 1-2% with GCC.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
subject: Copy ASCII strings in the view's dump with ensure_ascii (#5879)

author: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
message:
dump() now checks strings of up to 32 bytes against a table of the bytes
that can be written verbatim, four bytes per step, and copies them in one
go if all of them can. That is cheaper than setting up the vector scanner,
whose setup costs more than such a string takes to scan; SQLite's
jsonAppendString() writes strings with the same kind of table loop. Most
object keys and many values are this short (citm_catalog averages 8 bytes
per string, jeopardy 14).

GCC 16 and 13 stopped inlining put_indent() and put_literal() into the
pretty-printing loops once dump_escaped() had grown, which made indented
output up to 13% slower; both are now always inlined.

The new test puts every ASCII character and a 2-byte character at every
position of strings of 1 to 40 bytes and compares the output with the
reference implementation of the existing UTF-8 tests.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
subject: Copy short printable-ASCII strings without starting the scanner (#5878)

author: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
message:
json_sax_dom_parser::key() copied the key from the lexer's buffer into the
object. The lexer starts every token with an empty buffer (reset()), so the
key can be moved instead, which saves an allocation and a copy for every key
that does not fit into the string's inline buffer. json_sax_dom_parser
already moved string values the same way. ordered_map has no rvalue
operator[], so ordered_json still copies keys.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
subject: Move object keys into the value when parsing (#5855)

author: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
message:
* Match literals without a stack array and keep parser states in bytes

scan_after_whitespace() built the expected text of true, false, and null in
local std::array objects. With -fstack-protector-strong (the default of
Ubuntu's GCC, among others), a local array gives the function a stack canary
check, which then ran on every token. scan_literal() now takes the text
after the first character as a string literal, with its length as a template
parameter; for contiguous input it compares the rest at once and falls back
to the byte loop on a mismatch, so errors are reported at the same
character. It is out of line, which keeps the token dispatch small.

The parser kept the nesting of arrays and objects in a std::vector<bool>,
whose push_back() GCC calls out of line; it is a std::vector<std::uint8_t>
now.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Skip the literal fast path test without exceptions

The test case compares the error messages of both lexer paths, so it does
not compile with JSON_NOEXCEPTION (the caught exception does not exist).

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Allow the string literal parameter of scan_literal() for clang-tidy

The parameter takes the literal by array reference so that its length is
a template parameter; this is the same exemption the C array overloads of
to_json() and from_json() have.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

author: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
hunk_contexts: inline std::size_t valid_utf8_prefix(const unsigned char* data, std::size_t n) n
inline std::size_t scalar_string_bulk_run(const unsigned char* data, std::size_t
inline std::size_t find_string_delimiter(const unsigned char* data, std::size_t
inline std::size_t string_bulk_run(const unsigned char* data, std::size_t n) noe
message:
* Scan strings with SSE2, SSSE3, or NEON

The string fast path found the end of a run of plain characters 8 bytes at
a time (SWAR) and validated non-ASCII text one sequence at a time, calling
validate_one_utf8() out of line for each.

The vector code of json_view's scanner, in the new shared header
detail/input/simd_scan.hpp, now does both 16 bytes at a time: SSE2 finds
the end of a run on x86-64, and the UTF-8 check of Keiser and Lemire runs
with NEON on AArch64 and with SSSE3 on x86-64. SSSE3 is not part of x86-64,
so the check is compiled for it with a function attribute and used when the
CPU has it (cached in a constant-initialized atomic), else the scalar check;
code compiled with -mssse3 skips the CPU check. The first word of a run is
still checked with SWAR (the first four with NEON, where a vector mask
costs more), as most keys and short values end there, and the scalar
helpers are always inlined. On anything else, the scalar code is unchanged.

The new macro JSON_NO_SIMD selects the portable code everywhere, including
the SSE2/NEON digit formatting of the floating-point writer. The lexer tests
now also run with JSON_NO_SIMD and, on x86-64, with -mssse3, and a new test
places every byte that ends a run at each offset across several 16-byte
blocks, after ASCII and after CJK text.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Keep the string scan from slowing down short strings and dump() on Arm

Three benchmarks were 7-9% slower than develop on Apple M1 (Apple Clang,
-O3 -flto): Accept/jeopardy, Dump/citm_catalog, and Dump/jeopardy.

- dump(): the serializer passes a string without its closing quote, so
  plain_run_end() ran out of input and called the out-of-line NEON loop
  for every string, with fewer than 16 bytes left. The loop is now only
  called for 16 bytes or more.
- accept(): no string of jeopardy.json reaches the vector UTF-8 check,
  yet compiling it into the lexer's scan function made it 5% slower: the
  function runs once per token and now saved more registers and kept a
  stack slot. lexer_string_bulk_run() checks the first four words inline
  and continues out of line, and the serializer keeps string_bulk_run()
  inline, which is faster there.
- The byte that ends a run is read from the scanned buffer instead of
  through get(), which Apple Clang merged with the other get() calls that
  load the read position again right after it was stored (3%).

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Define string_bulk_run_from() only where lexer_string_bulk_run() calls it

With NEON and simdutf in C++17, lexer_string_bulk_run() takes the
string_bulk_run() path, so the out-of-line helper was unused.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Do not dispatch the SSSE3 string scan with GCC's C++20 modules

GCC does not keep the target("ssse3") attribute on functions it reads
back from a module interface, so the module build (ci_module_cpp20,
gcc:latest) rejected the intrinsics in vector_utf8_run() with "needs isa
option -mssse3". With __cpp_modules, GCC now uses the portable UTF-8 check
like other compilers without the target attribute; the SSE2 scan stays,
and -mssse3 or more still compiles the SSSE3 check directly. Clang is not
affected.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Include <cpuid.h> only once when json.hpp and json_view.hpp are both used

The SSSE3 dispatch of the string scan and the one of json_view each
include <cpuid.h>. Before GCC 11 the header has no include guard, so a
translation unit that includes both headers fails with GCC 10:
"redefinition of 'unsigned int __get_cpuid_max(unsigned int, unsigned int*)'".
Guard both includes with NLOHMANN_JSON_CPUID_INCLUDED.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Add an ABI tag for JSON_NO_SIMD

JSON_NO_SIMD selects between two definitions of the internal scanning and
formatting functions. Like JSON_VIEW_NO_SIMD (_vns), it now appends _ns to
the inline namespace, so translation units built with and without it can
be linked into one program without ODR violations.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

author: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
message:
After the digits are converted while scanning, copying the token text into
token_buffer (an out-of-line std::string::append) was about 10% of parsing
canada.json. The only reader is the string argument of
json_sax::number_float(), and the library's own handlers
(json_sax_dom_parser, json_sax_dom_callback_parser, json_sax_acceptor)
ignore it.

For contiguous input, the fast path now keeps a pointer to the token in the
input, and get_string() copies it on first use. The parser passes an empty
string to the handlers marked by the new internal trait
sax_ignores_number_text instead of calling get_string(), so json::parse()
and json::accept() never copy float text. User handlers, and
JSON_DIAGNOSTIC_POSITIONS (which reads get_string().size()), still see the
exact text. Keys and strings, which never have pending text, use the
unchecked get_string_token(). Input read through a window into a stream
(std::istream, FILE*) copies the text right away, because the next read may
refill the window.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
subject: Copy the text of float tokens only when a SAX handler asks for it (#5852)

author: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
hunk_contexts: inline bool has_nonzero_digit(const char* first, const char* last) noexcept
inline float_significand parse_float_significand(const char* first, const char*
message:
* Accumulate number digits while scanning them

The contiguous number fast path validated a token byte by byte, copied it
into token_buffer, and then converted it in out-of-line functions that
scanned the digits a second time: parse_float_native() called
parse_float_significand(), which returned its result through memory and
called std::any_of (out of line with GCC) twice per number, and
parse_integer_signed() divided by ten on every digit for its overflow check.

scan_number_bulk_contiguous() now accumulates the significand while it
validates the digits, eight at a time where at least eight bytes remain
(is_eight_digits() and parse_eight_digits(), after fast_float). Floats with
at most 19 digits go straight to decimal_to_float(); integers with at most
18 digits are stored without an overflow check (a narrower number type
still rejects values that do not round-trip). Longer tokens take the
existing path. has_nonzero_digit() is a plain loop and
parse_float_significand() is always inlined, which helps that path.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Skip the digit accumulation checks without exceptions

The section compares error messages from both lexer paths and parses
out-of-range numbers, so it does not compile (the caught exception does not
exist) and would abort with JSON_NOEXCEPTION.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Share the significant-digit loop of the integer part and the fraction

message:
With glibc and optimization, <stdio.h> turns getc_unlocked into an extern
inline function that reads the stdio buffer (fp->_IO_read_ptr) directly.
glibc, which is not instrumented, fills that buffer, so MemorySanitizer
treats the bytes as uninitialized and reports a false positive when the
parsers read from a FILE* (e.g., the fuzz harness FILE* leg, OSS-Fuzz
575915982). std::fgetc is an opaque call whose result MemorySanitizer treats
as initialized.

Select JSON_UNLOCKED_FILE_IO 0 when compiled with MemorySanitizer. This is a
regression from #5828 and not part of any release.

message:
* Write json_view's dump() without a call or conversion per token

The default dump() (no indentation, no ensure_ascii) gets its own
writer that makes the same walk and produces the same output:

- the write position stays in a local variable instead of a
  member, so the compiler keeps it in a register across stores
  through aliasing char pointers;
- strings and number tokens are copied with fixed-size 32-byte
  moves wherever enough source bytes remain, instead of one
  memcpy call per token;
- the innermost open container lives in local variables; a stack
  that starts as a local array of 32 entries holds the rest;
- unedited documents are walked through the node array in order,
  and integer tokens are read from the source directly.

On top of that, float tokens of at most 15 significant digits are
written straight from their digits via zmij::to_shortest() and
write_shortest(), without converting to a double and back: such
decimals are farther apart than a double's rounding interval, so
the token's digits are the double's shortest digits. Tokens of
16+ digits, or edited values, still go through decimal_to_float().
The view's own NEON write_decimal() is removed in favor of the
shared writer, and the dump output now grows in 64 KiB steps
instead of being resized to its estimate at once.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

Test the template options through enabled() so that conditions combined

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Fix out-of-bounds read when dumping a float token of an unchecked image

A float node of an image loaded with image_check::bounds can hold a

write_short_decimal(), which indexes its table of powers of ten by it:
an assertion failure in debug builds, an out-of-bounds read in release
builds. Use the counted overload only if the value has exactly that many
digits, otherwise count them.

message:
* Add images of json_documents: save() and load()

An image is a document stored so that loading it needs no
parsing: save() writes the node index, the text and the decoded
strings; the static load() reads an image written by save().

load() takes a pointer and size, a borrowed vector, or an owned
rvalue vector; the nodes are copied so they are aligned and can
be edited, while the text and decoded strings stay in the image.

image_check controls how much load() trusts the input: full
checks structure, bounds, strings and numbers, the parser's own
guarantees; bounds checks structure and bounds only; none skips
all checks, for images from a trusted source.

Layout is little-endian only ("NJVI" header, nodes, text, decoded
strings), following the idea of zero-copy formats such as
FlatBuffers and YaFF; the check follows FlatBuffers' Verifier.

New errors: parse_error.116 for a malformed image or a failed
check, type_error.320 for a discarded document or a big-endian
target.

A dedicated fuzzer and 6,000 seeded corruptions, checked under
ASan/UBSan, found and fixed two gaps: unchecked reserved header
fields, and unbounded null/boolean offsets that could make
dump() throw std::length_error.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Check each distinct string and float range once in the full image check

The structural walk now only collects the ranges; after it, each kind is sorted and checked once per distinct range. Ranges of one kind that overlap without being identical are rejected, as save() never writes them (nodes that share a value share the whole range). The cost is linear in the size of the image plus sorting the ranges.
